facts.claim: APR (annual percentage rate) is legally defined as "a measure of the cost of credit, expressed as a yearly rate, that relates the amount and timing of value received by the consumer to the amount and timing of payments made" — the closed-end credit definition in Regulation Z.
facts.source: 12 CFR 1026.22(a)(1), Regulation Z (eCFR) — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-12/chapter-X/part-1026/subpart-C/section-1026.22

facts.claim: APR disclosure is required by the Truth in Lending Act, enacted as Pub. L. 90-321, title I, May 29, 1968, 82 Stat. 149; the APR determination rule is 15 U.S.C. 1606.
facts.source: 15 U.S.C. 1606, source credit Pub. L. 90-321 §107, May 29, 1968 (U.S. House Office of the Law Revision Counsel) — https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title15-section1606&num=0&edition=prelim

facts.claim: A disclosed APR is legally "accurate" within a tolerance of 1/8 of 1 percentage point above or below the true rate for regular transactions, and 1/4 of 1 percentage point for irregular transactions (multiple advances, irregular payment periods or amounts).
facts.source: 12 CFR 1026.22(a)(2)-(3); 15 U.S.C. 1606(c) — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-12/chapter-X/part-1026/subpart-C/section-1026.22

facts.claim: Manifest gloss: APR is the "yearly cost of borrowing, including interest and fees." This is true for closed-end credit (mortgages, auto, personal loans) but NOT for credit cards. For open-end credit the APR is computed "by multiplying each periodic rate by the number of periods in a year" (1026.14(b)), and Regulation Z expressly excludes annual/participation fees from the finance charge (1026.4(c)(4)) — so a card's annual fee is disclosed separately and is not inside its APR.
facts.corrected_to: APR is the yearly cost of borrowing. On closed-end loans it folds in interest plus most loan fees (points, loan fees, finder's fees, credit insurance — 12 CFR 1026.4(b)). On a credit card, the APR is just the periodic interest rate annualized; the annual fee, late fees and over-limit fees are excluded from the finance charge and therefore are NOT in the APR.
facts.source: 12 CFR 1026.14(b) and 12 CFR 1026.4(a)-(c), Regulation Z (eCFR) — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-12/chapter-X/part-1026/subpart-A/section-1026.4

facts.claim: On a mortgage, the APR is higher than the interest rate because it "reflects the mortgage interest rate plus other charges" — points, mortgage broker fees and other charges to obtain the loan — while the interest rate alone "does not reflect fees or any other charges."
facts.source: CFPB Ask CFPB, "What is the difference between a mortgage interest rate and an APR?" — https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-the-difference-between-a-mortgage-interest-rate-and-an-apr-en-135/

facts.claim: The average credit card APR across all commercial-bank credit card accounts is 20.94%.
facts.source: Federal Reserve G.19 Consumer Credit, Terms of Credit — credit card plans, all accounts, Q2 2026; release dated 7 August 2026 — https://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/g19/current/

facts.claim: The average rate on credit card accounts that actually carried interest (accounts assessed interest) is 22.15%.
facts.source: Federal Reserve G.19 Consumer Credit, Terms of Credit — credit card plans, accounts assessed interest, Q2 2026; release dated 7 August 2026 — https://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/g19/current/

facts.claim: Course text (FL Stage 3, stage-3-rebuild.html): "The average credit card APR hit 21.5% in 2024 — a 40-year high." The 2024 figure is right (Q2 2024 = 21.51%, series peak 21.76% in Aug 2024), but "40-year high" is not supportable: the Federal Reserve's credit card rate series begins November 1994 with a documented break in series, so only ~31 years of data exist. It was a record high for the published series, not a 40-year high. The number is also now stale — the rate has fallen to 20.94% as of Q2 2026.
facts.corrected_to: The average credit card APR peaked at 21.76% in August 2024 — the highest in the Federal Reserve's series, which begins in November 1994. As of Q2 2026 it is 20.94%.
facts.source: Federal Reserve G.19 historical terms of credit, credit card plans (earliest observation 1994 Q4 = 15.69%, "break in series in November 1994") — https://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/g19/hist/cc_hist_tc_levels.html ; FRED TERMCBCCALLNS data table — https://fred.stlouisfed.org/data/TERMCBCCALLNS

facts.claim: A second, higher primary measure exists and should not be confused with the Fed's: CFPB reports the average APR on general purpose credit cards rose to about 25% in 2023 and was 24.9% in Q4 2024, with the average APR margin (APR minus prime) at a record 16.4% in 2024.
facts.source: CFPB, The Consumer Credit Card Market report to Congress (December 2025) — https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/cfpb_consumer-credit-card-market-report_2025.pdf

facts.claim: Course text (FL Stage 1, stage-1-survive.html): a payday loan at "400% APR." CFPB states a fee of $15 per $100 borrowed on a two-week loan "equates to an APR of almost 400 percent" — approximately 391% — and that payday fees run $10 to $30 per $100 borrowed depending on state law, with $15 per $100 being common.
facts.source: CFPB Ask CFPB, "What is an annual percentage rate (APR) and why is it higher than the interest rate for my payday loan?" — https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-an-annual-percentage-rate-apr-and-why-is-it-higher-than-the-interest-rate-for-my-payday-loan-en-1625/ ; "What are the costs and fees for a payday loan?" — https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-are-the-costs-and-fees-for-a-payday-loan-en-1589/

facts.claim: The Military Lending Act caps the Military Annual Percentage Rate (MAPR) at 36% on consumer credit to active-duty servicemembers and their dependents, and the MAPR must include credit insurance premiums, debt cancellation/suspension fees, ancillary product fees, finance charges, application fees and participation fees — "even if that charge would be excluded from the finance charge under Regulation Z."
facts.source: 32 CFR 232.4, Department of Defense, Limitations on terms of consumer credit extended to Service members and dependents (eCFR) — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-32/subtitle-A/chapter-I/subchapter-M/part-232/section-232.4

facts.claim: Federal credit unions are subject to an 18% APR ceiling on most loans, extended by the NCUA Board through 10 September 2027. The statutory default ceiling absent NCUA action is 15%.
facts.source: NCUA press release, "NCUA Board Extends Loan Interest Rate Ceiling," 6 February 2026 — https://ncua.gov/newsroom/press-release/2026/ncua-board-extends-loan-interest-rate-ceiling

facts.claim: The Credit CARD Act — which restricts APR increases on existing balances — is Public Law 111-24, enacted 22 May 2009.
facts.source: GovInfo, Public Law 111-24 (Credit Card Accountability Responsibility and Disclosure Act of 2009), approved May 22, 2009 — https://www.govinfo.gov/app/details/PLAW-111publ24

facts.claim: In a credit card application or solicitation (the "Schumer box"), the APR for purchases must be disclosed in at least 16-point type, with exceptions only for oral disclosures and penalty rates.
facts.source: 12 CFR 1026.60(b)(1), Regulation Z (eCFR) — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-12/chapter-X/part-1026/subpart-G/section-1026.60

facts.claim: APR is not APY. Regulation DD defines annual percentage yield as "a percentage rate reflecting the total amount of interest paid on an account, based on the interest rate and the frequency of compounding for a 365-day period," while an interest rate is "the annual rate of interest paid on an account which does not reflect compounding." APR governs what you pay to borrow (Reg Z); APY governs what a deposit account pays you (Reg DD).
facts.source: 12 CFR 1030.2, Regulation DD (eCFR) — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-12/chapter-X/part-1030/section-1030.2

facts.claim: Most credit card APRs are variable and are quoted as the prime rate plus a margin. The bank prime loan rate is 6.75%, so the 20.94% all-accounts average implies a margin of roughly 14.2 percentage points.
facts.source: Federal Reserve H.15 Selected Interest Rates, bank prime loan rate effective 7 August 2026 (page released 10 August 2026) — https://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/h15/

facts.claim: Course text (FL Stage 3): "Someone who carries a $5,000 balance at 21% and makes minimum payments will pay over $3,000 in interest before it's gone." The claim is true as a floor but badly understates the damage. Under the common minimum-payment formula (interest plus 1% of principal, $25 floor) $5,000 at 21% costs about $7,700 in interest over roughly 19 years; at a flat 3% of balance it is about $6,300 over ~16 years. Regulation Z leaves the minimum-payment formula to the issuer, so no single federal figure exists.
facts.source: Computed from the Regulation Z repayment-disclosure framework, 12 CFR Part 1026 Appendix M1 ("card issuers must use the minimum payment formula(s) that apply to a cardholder's account") — https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/m1/

facts.claim: Course text (FL Stage 2, stage-2-stabilize.html): "A 0% APR balance transfer card can pause interest for 12–21 months." CFPB's own market data describes introductory zero-percent APR offers running "between six and 21 months in duration" — the 21-month ceiling is right, but the floor is six months, not 12, so a reader shopping offers will see shorter promos than the course implies.
facts.corrected_to: Introductory 0% APR periods run roughly six to 21 months.
facts.source: CFPB, The Consumer Credit Card Market report to Congress (December 2025) — https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/cfpb_consumer-credit-card-market-report_2025.pdf

facts.claim: Course text (FL Stage 2): balance transfer fees are "usually 3–5%." No federal body publishes a balance-transfer-fee distribution; the CFPB 2025 Consumer Credit Card Market Report does not carry this figure. Do not state a range on primary-source authority.
facts.source: Searched CFPB, The Consumer Credit Card Market report to Congress (December 2025) — no balance transfer fee percentage published — https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/cfpb_consumer-credit-card-market-report_2025.pdf

facts.claim: Compound interest is 'interest paid on principal and on accumulated interest' — i.e. return earned on your original amount plus every return already earned (FL Stage 3, Module 05).
facts.source: SEC Investor.gov glossary entry, 'Compound Interest'. The SEC's exact wording is: "Interest paid on principal and on accumulated interest." This matches the course's plain-language framing and the manifest gloss 'Growth earned on your growth, not just your principal'. Note: the Investor.gov glossary page itself gives NO formula and NO worked example — if the glossary page wants to cite a government source for the formula, use Reg DD Appendix A (below), not this page.

facts.claim: By federal rule, a deposit account's Annual Percentage Yield (APY) already builds in compounding frequency, while the plain 'interest rate' does not — which is why APY is the number to compare.
facts.source: 12 CFR 1030.2(c) (Regulation DD, Truth in Savings, CFPB) via eCFR: "Annual percentage yield means a percentage rate reflecting the total amount of interest paid on an account, based on the interest rate and the frequency of compounding for a 365-day period and calculated according to the rules in appendix A of this part." 12 CFR 1030.4(b)(1) requires institutions to disclose BOTH "the 'annual percentage yield' and the 'interest rate,' using those terms." This is the single most useful legal rule for a compound-interest glossary page and the course does not currently state it.

facts.claim: The general APY formula fixed by federal regulation is APY = 100 [(1 + Interest/Principal)^(365/Days in term) − 1], assuming all principal and interest stay on deposit for the full term with no other transactions.
facts.source: 12 CFR Part 1030, Appendix A, Part I.A (Regulation DD, CFPB) via eCFR. Appendix A states the assumption explicitly: "all principal and interest remain on deposit for the entire term and that no other transactions (deposits or withdrawals) occur during the term." This is the closest thing to a government-published compounding formula and is a better citation than the commonly-used A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt), which no US regulator publishes.

facts.claim: A credit card's disclosed APR does NOT include compounding — it is the periodic rate multiplied by the number of periods in a year, so the rate you actually pay on a revolving balance is higher than the stated APR.
facts.source: 12 CFR 1026.14 (Regulation Z, Truth in Lending, CFPB) via eCFR: for open-end credit the annual percentage rate is "computed by multiplying each periodic rate by the number of periods in a year." A 1.5% monthly periodic rate discloses as 18% APR with no compounding adjustment. This is the exact mirror image of the Reg DD APY rule and is the sharpest way to make the course's 'same formula, opposite sign' point precise. Neither FL Stage 3 Module 05 nor Module 06 currently says this.

facts.claim: The average rate on credit card accounts assessed interest is 22.15% (FL Stage 3, Module 06 chart: 'Owed on a card at 22.15%', described as 'the Federal Reserve figure for accounts actually carrying a balance').
facts.source: Federal Reserve Board G.19 Consumer Credit statistical release, 'Commercial bank interest rates — Credit card plans, Accounts assessed interest', Q2 2026, released 7 August 2026. Independently confirmed at FRED series TERMCBCCINTNS (Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System), latest observation 22.15%, May 2026, last updated 8 July 2026. The Fed defines this as "the annualized ratio of total finance charges at all reporting banks to the total average daily balances against which the finance charges were assessed" — because it is already an annualized realized rate, the course's decision to compound it annually in the chart is defensible. The course's attribution of the figure to the Federal Reserve is correct and the figure is current as of today.

facts.claim: The rate across ALL credit card accounts (not just those carrying a balance) is 20.94% — the relevant contrast figure if the glossary page quotes 22.15%.
facts.source: Federal Reserve Board G.19 Consumer Credit release, 'Commercial bank interest rates — Credit card plans, All accounts', Q2 2026, released 7 August 2026. Defined by the Fed as "the stated APR averaged across all credit card accounts at all reporting banks." The course's separate illustrative '24% APR' example (FL Stage 3, Module 05) is above both published figures; it is framed as a hypothetical card rather than an average, so it is not an error, but a glossary page should not present 24% as the average.

facts.claim: Warren Buffett compounded at roughly 19.7% a year from 1965 to 2025 — sixty years (FL Stage 3, Module 05, '20% column' warning box).
facts.source: Berkshire Hathaway Inc. 2025 Annual Report, 'Berkshire's Performance vs. the S&P 500' table, first page: Compounded Annual Gain 1965–2025, Berkshire per-share market value = 19.7%; Overall Gain 1964–2025 = 6,099,294%. This is the original source — Berkshire publishes this table itself and files it with the SEC. Course figure is exact.

facts.claim: Over the same sixty years (1965–2025) the S&P 500 returned about 10.5% (FL Stage 3, Module 05).
facts.source: Berkshire Hathaway Inc. 2025 Annual Report, same performance table: Compounded Annual Gain 1965–2025, S&P 500 with dividends included = 10.5%; Overall Gain 1964–2025 = 46,061%. Course figure is exact, and the 'with dividends included' qualifier matters — a glossary page quoting 10.5% should carry it.

facts.claim: Buffett tells ordinary investors to buy index funds rather than try to copy him (FL Stage 3, Module 05).
facts.source: Berkshire Hathaway 2013 Shareholder Letter (berkshirehathaway.com/letters/2013ltr.pdf), Buffett describing the instructions in his own will for the trustee managing money left to his wife: "Put 10% of the cash in short-term government bonds and 90% in a very low-cost S&P 500 index fund. (I suggest Vanguard's.)" He adds that for non-professionals "a low-cost S&P 500 index fund will achieve this goal" and that "the 'know-nothing' investor who both diversifies and keeps his costs minimal is virtually certain to get satisfactory results." The course's attribution is accurate and this letter is the primary citation to use.

facts.claim: Inflation has averaged around 3% per year historically (FL Stage 3, Module 04).
facts.source: Calculated directly from BLS Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U), U.S. city average, all items, 1982-84=100, annual-average index values published in the BLS Historical CPI-U supplemental table: 1926 annual average = 17.7, 2023 annual average = 304.702. That is a compound annual rate of 2.98% over 97 years. The course's 'around 3%' is accurate for the century-scale framing it uses. Caveat worth stating on the glossary page: over the shorter 1965–2023 window the same BLS series gives 3.99%/yr, so the 3% figure depends on starting in the 1920s.

facts.claim: The broad U.S. market has averaged roughly 10% a year before inflation and roughly 7% after it (FL Stage 3, Module 05, 'Plan on 7%. Be delighted by 10.').
facts.source: Cross-derived from two primary sources: Berkshire Hathaway 2025 Annual Report (S&P 500 with dividends, 10.5% compounded annually 1965–2025) and BLS CPI-U annual averages (2.98%/yr 1926–2023). Geometric real return of 10.0% nominal against 2.95% inflation = 6.85%, which rounds to the course's 7%. The pairing is internally consistent. Note that against the higher 1965–2025 inflation rate (3.94%/yr) the real return on a 10.5% nominal is 6.3%, not 7% — so the 10%/7% pair should be presented as the century-scale figures the course explicitly frames them as, not as a 60-year result.

facts.claim: The most recent 12-month CPI inflation reading is 3.5%.
facts.source: BLS Consumer Price Index news release, June 2026: CPI-U "rose 3.5 percent over the last 12 months, not seasonally adjusted." Needed if the glossary page contrasts today's inflation against the long-run 3% average or against deposit yields.

facts.claim: The Rule of 72: divide 72 by your annual return to estimate years to double; at 7% that is about 10 years (FL Stage 3, Module 05).
facts.source: Verified mathematically rather than by publication, because it is a heuristic with no issuing body. 72/7 = 10.29 years; the exact answer is ln(2)/ln(1.07) = 10.24 years — the shortcut is off by about 0.6%, so 'about 10 years' is correct. The course makes no attribution for the rule (it does not name Pacioli or anyone else), so there is no attribution claim to check. If the glossary page adds an attribution, it will need its own sourcing; the rule's accuracy degrades outside roughly the 6–10% band.

facts.claim: $250/month for 30 years, compounded monthly, produces $173,512 at 4%, $304,993 at 7%, $565,122 at 10%, $1,730,820 at 15% and $5,744,459 at 20%, on $90,000 contributed (FL Stage 3, Module 05 table).
facts.source: Recomputed independently with the standard ordinary-annuity future-value formula FV = PMT × [((1+r/12)^(12t) − 1)/(r/12)]. Every one of the five figures reproduces to the dollar. The growth-share column (48%, 70%, 84%, 95%, 98%) also checks out. Same verification passes for the $100/month years table and the start-age delay table ($1,581,020 at 25, $949,160 at 30, $565,122 at 35, $331,708 at 40, $189,842 at 45).

facts.claim: The $250/month table footnote states the money is '$250/month contributed at the start of each month, compounded monthly'.
facts.corrected_to: The figures are end-of-month (ordinary annuity) contributions, not start-of-month. Start-of-month (annuity-due) contributions at the same rates would give $174,091 / $306,772 / $569,831 / $1,752,455 / $5,840,200 — every published number is lower than that and matches the end-of-month formula exactly. Fix is one word in the footnote: change 'at the start of each month' to 'at the end of each month'. Do not change the numbers; they are right and are used consistently across all three tables and both stages.
facts.source: Recomputed both annuity conventions from first principles. The end-of-month formula reproduces all five table values to the dollar; the start-of-month formula reproduces none of them. Confirmed the same end-of-month convention is used in the $100/month table (10yr@4% = $14,725) and the start-age table, so this is a footnote wording error, not a calculation error.

facts.claim: Someone investing $200/month from 25 to 35 and then stopping ends with $280,968 at 65, versus $243,994 for someone investing $200/month from 35 to 65 — the earlier saver puts in a third of the money and finishes about $37,000 ahead, at 7% (FL Stage 3, Module 05).
facts.source: Recomputed independently: $200/month end-of-month for 10 years at 7% compounded monthly = $34,617, grown a further 30 years at 7%/12 = $280,968. $200/month for 30 years at 7% = $243,994. Difference $36,974, i.e. 'about $37,000'. Both figures reproduce to the dollar. This is the strongest single illustration on the page and it is arithmetically sound.

facts.claim: $200/month in an S&P 500 index fund at the historical average return over 30 years grows to approximately $407,000, of which $72,000 is out of pocket and $335,000 is compound growth (FL Stage 4, Module 10).
facts.corrected_to: At the 10% 'historical average return' the course itself uses everywhere else, $200/month for 30 years compounded monthly is approximately $452,100 — of which $72,000 is contributed and $380,100 is growth. The published $407,000 implies a 9.50% return, which appears nowhere else in the course. This also contradicts FL Stage 3 Module 05, where $250/month for 30 years at 10% is correctly given as $565,122; scaling that to $200/month gives $452,098, not $407,000. Either raise the figure to ~$452,000 and the growth line to ~$380,000, or state the 9.5% assumption explicitly.
facts.source: Recomputed with the same end-of-month annuity formula that reproduces every other table in the course to the dollar, and cross-checked against the course's own $250/month@10% figure. Underlying 10% assumption is itself supported by Berkshire Hathaway's 2025 Annual Report (S&P 500 with dividends, 10.5% compounded 1965–2025). The internal inconsistency is the finding — one of these two numbers has to move.

facts.claim: $5,000 owed on a card at 22.15% reaches $36,975 in ten years, while $5,000 in the market at 10% reaches $12,969 (FL Stage 3, Module 06 chart, plus the year-by-year table).
facts.source: Recomputed: 5000 × 1.2215^10 = $36,975 and 5000 × 1.10^10 = $12,969, both exact, and all the intermediate year-2/4/6/8 values in the disclosed table reproduce as well. One caveat for the glossary page: this compounds the card rate ANNUALLY. Real cards compound monthly or daily, which on a 22.15% nominal rate would reach $44,891 over ten years — so the chart, if anything, understates the debt side. Because the Fed's 'accounts assessed interest' series is already an annualized realized ratio of finance charges to balances, annual compounding is the defensible reading; but do not re-describe 22.15% as an 'APR' compounded monthly, because that would double-count.

facts.claim: The magic penny doubling daily for 30 days reaches $5,368,709.12 on day 30, having been at $5,242.88 on day 20 and $1,342,177.28 on day 28 (FL Stage 4, Module 10).
facts.source: Recomputed: $0.01 × 2^29 = $5,368,709.12 exactly; day 20 = 0.01 × 2^19 = $5,242.88; day 28 = 0.01 × 2^27 = $1,342,177.28. Every row of the table is exact. The course already labels it 'a mathematical illustration, not a market prediction', which is the correct disclaimer to carry across to the glossary page.

facts.claim: $1,000 invested at birth at a 10% historical average return is approximately $5,560 by age 18 (FL Stage 4, Module 11).
facts.source: Recomputed: 1000 × 1.10^18 = $5,560 exactly, using annual compounding. Note the compounding convention differs from the rest of the course (monthly) — with monthly compounding the same inputs give $6,005. Worth standardising if the glossary page reuses this figure.

facts.claim: Adding $100/month through childhood reaches approximately $61,000 by age 18, and that $61,000 left invested from 18 to 65 at a 7% real return becomes approximately $1.6 million (FL Stage 4, Module 11).
facts.corrected_to: The two figures use different compounding conventions and do not chain cleanly. $100/month for 18 years at 10% compounded monthly is $60,056 on its own — the '$61,000' evidently counts only the monthly contributions and silently drops the $1,000 birth seed, which would add $5,560–$6,005 for a true total of roughly $65,600. And $61,000 compounded from 18 to 65 (47 years) at 7% gives $1.47 million with annual compounding; the stated $1.6 million only appears with monthly compounding ($1.62 million). Pick one convention — monthly, to match the rest of the course — and restate as roughly $65,600 by age 18 growing to roughly $1.74 million by 65.
facts.source: Recomputed all four variants (seed included/excluded × annual/monthly compounding) with the same formulas that reproduce the Stage 3 tables exactly. No combination produces both $61,000 and $1.6 million simultaneously. This is a smaller error than the $407,000 one but sits in the same family: the compounding convention drifts between modules.

facts.claim: A savings account yielding 4.5% might net you about 3% in real purchasing power after taxes and inflation; the course's table also labels 4% as 'a good savings account' (FL Stage 3, Module 04 and Module 05).
facts.corrected_to: The FDIC national deposit rate for savings accounts is 0.38% as of July 2026 — roughly one twelfth of the 4.5% figure. 4%–4.5% describes competitive online high-yield savings accounts, not a typical savings account. The course hedges with 'might', so this is not a flat error, but a glossary page must not state 4.5% unqualified. Recommended framing: 'the FDIC national average savings rate is 0.38% (July 2026); high-yield online accounts pay several percentage points more, which is the entire reason the distinction matters.'
facts.source: FDIC National Rates and Rate Caps, National Rate: Savings, July 2026 = 0.38%, retrieved via FRED series SNDR (source organization: Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation; last updated 22 July 2026). The FDIC's own national-rates pages returned HTTP 403 to direct fetching, so the figure was taken from the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis's redistribution of the FDIC series rather than from fdic.gov directly.

facts.claim: $1,000 invested in the S&P 500 in 1980 with dividends reinvested became approximately $150,000+ by 2025, with most of that growth in the last 15 years (FL Stage 4, Module 10).
facts.source: Could not confirm against a primary source. S&P Dow Jones Indices — the index publisher and therefore the primary body — does not expose a 1980-to-date total-return figure on its public S&P 500 page, and the S&P 500 Total Return index series is behind its data licensing. The claim implies an 11.78% compound annual total return over 45 years, which is plausible but above the 10.5% that Berkshire's 2025 Annual Report reports for 1965–2025, so it is not self-evidently right either. Recommend either dropping this figure from the glossary page or replacing it with the Berkshire-sourced 10.5% since 1965, which is verifiable. The secondary trailing claim that 'most of that growth happened in the last 15 years' is a mathematical property of any compounding curve and needs no separate sourcing.

facts.claim: Paying off a credit card balance is a guaranteed, tax-free, risk-free return equal to the card's rate — clearing a $3,000 balance at 22% earns exactly 22% (FL Stage 3, Module 06), and no legal investment reliably offers that.
facts.source: This is an arithmetic identity rather than a published statistic: avoiding an interest charge of r on a balance is numerically identical to earning r on the same amount, and because it is an avoided expense rather than income it is not taxable. The 'no legal investment reliably offers 22%' half is supported by Berkshire Hathaway's 2025 Annual Report, which shows that the single most celebrated long-run record in finance — Buffett's own, 1965–2025 — is 19.7%, below the current 22.15% card rate on accounts assessed interest (Federal Reserve G.19, Q2 2026). That juxtaposition is the strongest verifiable version of the claim and both halves of it are primary-sourced.

facts.claim: A credit score is a 300–850 number lenders use to predict how likely you are to repay. (Manifest gloss; FL Stage 1 Module 04: 'Your credit score (300–850) tells lenders how likely you are to repay money.')
facts.source: CFPB, 'What is a credit score?' — 'A credit score is a prediction of your credit behavior, such as how likely you are to pay a loan back on time' and scores 'typically span from 300 to 850.' Corroborated by FICO's own consumer site: 'FICO Scores generally range from 300 to 850.'

facts.claim: Glossary precision point: 300–850 is not universal. CFPB: 'Many scores range from 300 to 850, but different companies use different ranges.' FICO notes some industry-specific score types (auto, bankcard) use a broader range.
facts.source: CFPB 'Understand your credit score'; ficoscore.com FAQs ('some score types have slightly broader ranges')

facts.claim: The five FICO factors and their weights: Payment History 35%, Amounts Owed 30%, Length of Credit History 15%, Credit Mix 10%, New Credit 10%. (FL Stage 1 Module 04 states exactly these.)
facts.source: myFICO, 'How are FICO Scores Calculated?' — FICO is the model's author, so this is primary. Caveat FICO states and the course omits: 'The percentages shown are for the general population and may be different for different credit profiles.'

facts.claim: FICO score tiers: 300–579 Poor, 580–669 Fair, 670–739 Good, 740–799 Very Good, 800–850 Exceptional. This validates the course's Stage 3 action step 'once your credit score is above 670' as the Good threshold.
facts.source: ficoscore.com, 'FAQs About FICO Scores in the US' (Fair Isaac's own consumer site)

facts.claim: Keep credit utilization below 30% of your total credit limit. (FL Stage 1 Module 04: 'Keep it below 30%.')
facts.source: CFPB, 'How do I get and keep a good credit score?' — 'Experts advise keeping your use of credit at no more than 30 percent of your total credit limit.' (page reviewed Dec 12, 2024)

facts.claim: 'Below 10% is ideal' for credit utilization. (FL Stage 1 Module 04.)
facts.source: No primary source states a 10% threshold. CFPB publishes only the 30% figure; FICO's 'Amounts Owed' page gives no numeric target. Widely repeated by secondary sites but not set or published by CFPB, FICO, or VantageScore. Recommend the glossary state 30% as the sourced threshold and present 'lower is better' qualitatively rather than as a published number.

facts.claim: You can get a free credit report from all three nationwide bureaus weekly at AnnualCreditReport.com, and it is the only federally authorized site. (FL Stage 1 Module 04 and Stage 3 Module 01.)
facts.corrected_to: Weekly access is real and permanent, but the legal entitlement is narrower than 'you're entitled to.' FCRA 15 U.S.C. §1681j(a)(1)(A) entitles a consumer to one free file disclosure 'once during any 12-month period upon request.' Weekly free access is a voluntary program the three bureaus have permanently extended, not a statutory right — the bureaus could in principle narrow it back to the statutory annual minimum. Accurate phrasing: 'Federal law guarantees one free report per bureau every 12 months; the three bureaus have permanently extended that to one per week.'
facts.source: 15 U.S.C. §1681j(a)(1)(A) (Cornell LII); FTC Consumer Advice, 'Free Credit Reports' — 'All three nationwide credit bureaus have permanently extended a program that lets you check your credit report from each once a week for free at AnnualCreditReport.com' and 'Only one website — AnnualCreditReport.com — is authorized to fill orders for the free annual credit reports you are entitled to by law.'

facts.claim: 'Roughly 1 in 5 credit reports contains an error significant enough to affect your score, according to FTC research.' (FL Stage 3 Module 01.)
facts.corrected_to: Two errors in one sentence. The FTC's 2013 study (1,001 participants, 2,968 reports) found (a) one in five CONSUMERS had an error on at least one of their three reports — not one in five reports — and (b) the share with errors serious enough to matter was FIVE PERCENT, not 20%: 'Five percent of consumers had errors on one of their three major credit reports that could lead to them paying more for products such as auto loans and insurance.' Separately, 'slightly more than one in 10 consumers saw a change in their credit score after the CRAs modified errors,' and 'four out of five consumers who filed disputes experienced some modification to their credit report.' Accurate phrasing: 'In an FTC study, one in five consumers had an error on at least one of their three credit reports, and one in twenty had an error serious enough to cost them money on a loan or insurance.'
facts.source: FTC press release, 'In FTC Study, Five Percent of Consumers Had Errors on Their Credit Reports That Could Result in Less Favorable Terms for Loans,' February 11, 2013

facts.claim: Credit bureaus have 30 days to investigate a dispute and respond. (FL Stage 3 Module 01.)
facts.source: 15 U.S.C. §1681i(a)(1) (Cornell LII) — reinvestigation must complete 'before the end of the 30-day period beginning on the date on which the agency receives the notice of the dispute.' Worth adding to the glossary: the 30 days 'may be extended for not more than 15 additional days if the consumer reporting agency receives information from the consumer during that 30-day period that is relevant to the reinvestigation' — a 45-day maximum.

facts.claim: Late payments and collections generally fall off your report after 7 years from the original delinquency date. (FL Stage 3 Module 02.)
facts.source: 15 U.S.C. §1681c(a)(4) — 'Accounts placed for collection or charged to profit and loss which antedate the report by more than seven years.' Precision note from §1681c(c)(1): the seven-year clock actually begins 'upon the expiration of the 180-day period beginning on the date of the commencement of the delinquency,' so the true outside limit is roughly seven years plus 180 days.

facts.claim: 'Chapter 7 bankruptcy stays 10 years; Chapter 13 stays 7.' (FL Stage 3 Module 02.)
facts.corrected_to: The 10-year figure is statutory; the 7-year figure is not. FCRA 15 U.S.C. §1681c(a)(1) sets a single 10-year limit for ALL bankruptcies — 'Cases under title 11 ... that, from the date of entry of the order for relief or the date of adjudication ... antedate the report by more than 10 years' — with no distinction between Chapter 7 and Chapter 13. The 7-year removal of completed Chapter 13 filings is a voluntary policy of the nationwide credit bureaus, not a legal requirement. Accurate phrasing: 'Federal law lets any bankruptcy stay on your report for up to 10 years. In practice the bureaus remove a completed Chapter 13 after 7 years as a matter of their own policy — that is a courtesy, not a right you can enforce.'
facts.source: 15 U.S.C. §1681c(a)(1) (Cornell LII)

facts.claim: 'One late payment can drop your score 50–100 points.' (FL Stage 1 Module 04.)
facts.corrected_to: No FICO primary source supports a universal 50–100 point figure, and FICO's own material cuts against the framing. myFICO's payment-history page states: 'A few late payments are not an automatic score-killer. An overall good credit history can outweigh one or two instances of late credit card payments.' FICO's blog 'How Credit Actions Impact FICO Scores' (June 4, 2019, FICO Score 9) declines to publish standardized point drops, stating 'the impact to FICO Score of a given credit action is highly dependent on the starting credit profile of the consumer.' Accurate phrasing: 'A missed payment is the single most damaging routine credit event, and the higher your score is to begin with, the more points you lose. FICO does not publish a fixed number, because the drop depends on your starting profile.'
facts.source: myFICO, 'How Payment History Impacts Your Credit Score'; FICO blog, 'How Credit Actions Impact FICO Scores' (2019-06-04)

facts.claim: Each credit application causes a hard inquiry that temporarily dips your score. (FL Stage 1 Module 04 and Stage 3 Module 03.)
facts.source: myFICO, 'Credit Checks and Inquiries' — quantified figures the glossary should carry: 'one additional credit inquiry will take less than five points off their FICO Scores'; inquiries stay on the report 'up to two years, but they only affect the FICO Scores for a year'; rate-shopping for the same loan type is deduplicated within 'any 14-day span' (older FICO versions) or 'any 45-day span' (newer versions); and 'FICO Scores ignore inquiries made in the 30 days prior to scoring' for mortgage, auto, and student loans. CFPB corroborates the 30-day and 14–45 day windows.

facts.claim: Accurate negative information cannot legally be removed early, and a credit repair company that guarantees a specific score increase is a red flag under the Credit Repair Organizations Act. (FL Stage 3 Module 01.)
facts.source: 15 U.S.C. §1679b (Cornell LII) — CROA prohibits statements that are 'untrue or misleading' about a consumer's creditworthiness, and §1679b(b) bars charging in advance: 'No credit repair organization may charge or receive any money or other valuable consideration for the performance of any service ... before such service is fully performed.' The advance-fee ban is the sharper consumer-facing test and is worth adding to the glossary alongside the guarantee red flag.

facts.claim: You can opt out of pre-screened credit offers for five years, free, at OptOutPrescreen.com — the official site named in the Fair Credit Reporting Act. (FL Stage 3 Module 02.)
facts.source: FTC Consumer Advice, 'What To Know About Prescreened Offers for Credit and Insurance' — optoutprescreen.com or 1-888-5-OPT-OUT (1-888-567-8688) opts you out 'for five years'; a permanent opt-out requires signing and returning the Permanent Opt-Out Election form obtained online. Requests are processed within five days.

facts.claim: The average US FICO Score is 714. (Not currently stated in the course; a 2026 glossary page should carry it.)
facts.source: FICO (Fair Isaac Corporation) investor newsroom, 'FICO Score Credit Insights Report: Average FICO Score Dips to 714,' released March 24, 2026 — down 2 points year over year and on a downward trend since 2023, driven by resumed student-loan delinquency reporting and rising mortgage delinquencies. Also from the same release: 48.1% of US consumers now score 750 or higher, up from 43.3% in 2019.

facts.claim: There are three nationwide credit bureaus — Equifax, Experian, TransUnion — and you have more than one credit score, not one.
facts.source: CFPB, 'Understand your credit score' — 'The three biggest are Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion' and 'You can have more than one score, because: Lenders use different scores for different products; There are many different credit scoring formulas; Information can come from different credit reporting sources.'

facts.claim: VantageScore uses the same 300–850 range as FICO.
facts.source: VantageScore's own consumer FAQ (vantagescore.com/consumers/consumer-faqs) — 'Scores usually range from 300 to 850.' Note: the FAQ states this generally and does not break the range out by model version, so the glossary should not attribute the range specifically to VantageScore 4.0 without the model's user guide.

facts.claim: 'Under current federal rules, medical debt is treated differently by credit reporting agencies than other debt.' (FL Stage 1, medical-bills passage.)
facts.corrected_to: There is no federal rule doing this as of 11 August 2026. The CFPB finalized a rule on January 7, 2025 to ban medical bills from credit reports, but a US District Court VACATED it on July 11, 2025, holding it 'exceeded the Bureau's statutory authority and was contrary to the Fair Credit Reporting Act' — the CFPB's own page now carries that banner. What still applies is a VOLUNTARY change by Equifax, Experian and TransUnion: all paid medical collections removed, unpaid medical collections under $500 removed (effective April 11, 2023), and a one-year wait from the date of service before any unpaid medical debt can appear. Accurate phrasing: 'The three bureaus voluntarily removed paid medical collections and unpaid ones under $500, and wait a year before reporting any medical debt. That is bureau policy, not federal law — the CFPB rule that would have made it law was struck down in July 2025.'
facts.source: CFPB, 'CFPB Finalizes Rule to Remove Medical Bills from Credit Reports' (archived, carries the vacatur banner dated July 11, 2025); CFPB blog, 'Have medical debt? Anything already paid or under $500 should no longer be on your credit report'

facts.claim: Credit utilization is the balance reported on a revolving account divided by that account's credit limit ($300 ÷ $1,000 = 30%).
facts.source: myFICO, 'How FICO Scores Look at Credit Card Limits' — 'credit utilization rate is calculated by dividing an account's outstanding balance by its credit limit'; CFPB, 'Does it hurt my credit to close a credit card?' — 'the amount of credit you're using, divided by the total amount you have available'

facts.claim: 'Amounts owed' — the category credit utilization dominates — is approximately 30% of a FICO Score.
facts.source: FICO Score Fact Sheet (fico.com/en/resource-access/download/4292): 'Amount Owed — approximately 30% of a FICO Score'

facts.claim: Payment history is approximately 35% of a FICO Score; length of credit history 15%; new credit 10%; types of credit (mix) 10%.
facts.source: FICO Score Fact Sheet; myFICO 'How are FICO Scores Calculated?' — 35/30/15/10/10

facts.claim: FICO Scores most often fall within a 300–850 range.
facts.source: FICO Score Fact Sheet: 'FICO Scores most often fall within a 300–850 score range'

facts.claim: Course text: 'Keep it below 30%.' The 30% figure is expert guidance, not a scoring threshold — there is no cliff at 30%.
facts.source: CFPB, 'How do I get and keep a good credit score?' — 'Experts advise keeping your use of credit at no more than 30 percent of your total credit limit'; myFICO, 'What Should My Credit Utilization Ratio Be?' — 'the data doesn't support the implication that your credit score will dip once your utilization ratio crosses the 30% threshold'

facts.claim: Course text: 'Below 10% is ideal.' FICO states this in its own words.
facts.source: myFICO, 'What Should My Credit Utilization Ratio Be?' — 'Generally, keeping it below 10% (and consistently paying bills on time) can help you build and maintain a good FICO Score'

facts.claim: Utilization applies to revolving accounts (credit cards, lines of credit) only — installment debt such as car and student loans does not count toward it.
facts.source: myFICO, 'How Owing Money Can Impact Your Credit Score' — 'Your credit utilization ratio on revolving accounts—the percentage of your available credit you're using—is an important factor in your FICO Scores'; VantageScore, 'Credit Utilization Ratio' knowledge-center article (revolving accounts only)

facts.claim: Utilization is measured both per card and across all cards combined, and both are scored — so a single maxed card is a separate negative signal even when the aggregate ratio looks healthy.
facts.source: myFICO, 'What Should My Credit Utilization Ratio Be?' — calculates both an individual per-card ratio and an aggregate ratio; VantageScore knowledge-center article — 'total utilization across all cards, calculating individual account ratios'

facts.claim: Card issuers report the balance to the bureaus based on the statement closing balance, not the balance after the due-date payment — which is why paying before the statement closes lowers reported utilization.
facts.source: myFICO, 'What Should My Credit Utilization Ratio Be?' — 'Credit card companies typically report card balances to the credit reporting agencies based on your balance each month when your statement closes'; VantageScore — 'typically monthly statement balances rather than current balances'

facts.claim: Blog text: the due date is 'roughly three weeks' after the statement closing date. This is the federal regulatory minimum, not merely an issuer habit.
facts.source: Regulation Z, 12 CFR 1026.5(b)(2)(ii) — periodic statements must be 'mailed or delivered at least 21 days prior to the payment due date' (and 21 days before any grace period expires)

facts.claim: Blog text: 'Consumers around a 800 FICO average roughly 7%' utilization.
facts.source: myFICO blog, 'The Traits of the 800 FICO Credit Score Holder' — 'On average, "exceptional" credit score holders use about 7% of their available credit'
facts.asOf: 2017-03-08 (FICO's own figure; FICO has not republished it since — label the year on the page)

facts.claim: The national average credit card utilization rate is 35.5%.
facts.source: FICO Score Credit Insights Report (inaugural), published 16 September 2025 — average credit card utilization rate 35.5%. FICO's 24 March 2026 update did not restate the figure.

facts.claim: The average U.S. FICO Score is 714 (down from 715), with 48.1% of consumers at 750 or higher.
facts.source: FICO Score Credit Insights Report, published 24 March 2026 — average FICO Score 714; 48.1% of U.S. consumers at 750+, up from 43.3% in 2019

facts.claim: Closing a credit card raises your utilization ratio (it removes that card's limit from your available credit) and can lower your score.
facts.source: CFPB, 'Does it hurt my credit to close a credit card?' — 'Closing an existing card can increase your credit utilization ratio and lower your score'

facts.claim: You do not need to carry a balance to build or keep a good score.
facts.source: CFPB, 'How do I get and keep a good credit score?' — 'You don't need to carry a balance on credit cards to get a good score'; CFPB credit-score-myths blog — 'Paying off your credit cards in full every month is the best way to improve a credit score'

facts.claim: Consumers can get a free credit report from each of the three nationwide bureaus every week at AnnualCreditReport.com, and this is permanent.
facts.source: FTC Consumer Advice alert, 'You now have permanent access to free weekly credit reports' (13 October 2023) — 'The program was extended twice and is now permanent'

facts.claim: Course text (Stage 3): 'Roughly 1 in 5 credit reports contains an error significant enough to affect your score, according to FTC research.' This merges two separate FTC findings into one wrong number.
facts.corrected_to: The FTC's 2013 study found 1 in 5 consumers had an error on at least one of their three credit reports; only 5% (1 in 20) had errors serious enough to result in less favorable loan or insurance terms. Sample: 1,001 participants, 2,968 reports. Rewrite as: 'About 1 in 5 consumers has an error on at least one of their three reports, and about 1 in 20 has one serious enough to cost them money.'
facts.source: FTC press release, 'In FTC Study, Five Percent of Consumers Had Errors on Their Credit Reports That Could Result in Less Favorable Terms for Loans' (11 February 2013)

facts.claim: Course text (Stage 1): 'One late payment can drop your score 50–100 points.'
facts.corrected_to: The drop depends heavily on the starting score, and 50–100 is wrong at the low end. FICO's own published simulation: a 30-day late took a 793 score to 710–730 (a 63–83 point drop) and a 607 score to 570–590 (a 17–37 point drop). Rewrite as: 'A single 30-day late can cost roughly 15–35 points from a mid-600s score and 60–85 points from a high-700s score — the cleaner your history, the more it hurts.' This matters because the 607 case is the reader this course is written for.
facts.source: myFICO, 'How Credit Actions Impact FICO Scores' (FICO's own damage-point simulation, Sophia 607 and Maria 793 profiles)

facts.claim: Course text (Stage 3): 'Chapter 7 bankruptcy stays 10 years; Chapter 13 stays 7.' The 7-year Chapter 13 figure is not what the statute says.
facts.corrected_to: The FCRA sets a single 10-year limit for all 'cases under title 11' — it does not distinguish Chapter 7 from Chapter 13. The 7-year removal of Chapter 13 is a voluntary policy of the credit bureaus, not a legal right. State it as bureau practice, not law. The 7-year limit for collections, charge-offs and other adverse items IS statutory.
facts.source: Fair Credit Reporting Act § 605, 15 U.S.C. § 1681c(a)(1)–(4), FTC-published text revised March 2026 — title 11 cases 'more than 10 years'; 'accounts placed for collection or charged to profit and loss which antedate the report by more than seven years'; 'any other adverse item of information ... more than seven years'

facts.claim: Course text (Stage 3): 'Bureaus have 30 days to investigate and respond.' True but incomplete.
facts.corrected_to: 30 days, extendable to 45 — the 30-day period 'may be extended for not more than 15 additional days if the consumer reporting agency receives information from the consumer during that 30-day period that is relevant to the reinvestigation.' Say '30 days, up to 45 if you send more documents mid-dispute' so readers don't think a 40-day response is a violation.
facts.source: Fair Credit Reporting Act § 611, 15 U.S.C. § 1681i(a)(1)(A)–(B)

facts.claim: Course text: a credit repair company guaranteeing a specific score increase is a red flag under the Credit Repair Organizations Act.
facts.source: Credit Repair Organizations Act, 15 U.S.C. § 1679b(a)(1) — prohibits any 'statement ... which is untrue or misleading' about a consumer's creditworthiness, credit standing or credit capacity; § 1679b(b) — 'No credit repair organization may charge or receive any money or other valuable consideration for the performance of any service' before the service is fully performed. The advance-fee ban is the cleaner, more checkable rule to cite.

facts.claim: Blog text: the average credit card rate used in the compounding chart is 22.15%.
facts.source: Federal Reserve G.19 Consumer Credit release, series TERMCBCCINTNS (Commercial Bank Interest Rate on Credit Card Plans, Accounts Assessed Interest) via FRED — 22.15%
facts.asOf: 2026-05 (latest observation; series is quarterly — Feb/May/Aug/Nov — so re-check after the August 2026 print)

facts.claim: Supporting context figure if the page cites a card APR: the CFPB reports a higher average because it measures a different thing.
facts.source: CFPB, 'The Consumer Credit Card Market' (December 2025) — average general-purpose card APR 25.2% and private label 31.3% in 2024, 'the highest levels since at least 2015'; the Fed's 22.15% covers only accounts assessed interest at commercial banks. Do not present the two as interchangeable.

facts.claim: VantageScore weights utilization differently from FICO — the blog's disclaimer says so and that is accurate.
facts.source: VantageScore, 'Credit Utilization Ratio: The Lesser Known Key to Your Credit Health' — the ratio 'can account for up to 30% of your credit score'; recommends 'at or below 30% of their assigned credit limits' and single digits for an excellent score

facts.claim: FICO Scores are used in 90% of U.S. lending decisions — useful for establishing why FICO's weights are the ones to quote.
facts.source: FICO Score Fact Sheet — 'FICO Scores are used in 90% US of lending decisions'

facts.claim: Blog text: utilization 'has no memory' — it is recalculated from scratch every time your balance is reported, and last month's 90% is not averaged in.
facts.source: No FICO or VantageScore publication states this in those terms. The closest primary support is the FICO Score Fact Sheet: FICO Scores are a snapshot that 'change only when credit report information changes.' The mechanism is right but the phrasing is folk wisdom from the myFICO user forums, not a FICO statement. Recommend rephrasing to FICO's own snapshot language rather than sourcing 'no memory' to FICO.

facts.claim: Blog text: reporting 0% on every card scores slightly worse than reporting a small balance (1–9%) on one card.
facts.source: Neither FICO nor VantageScore publishes this. FICO says only that low utilization helps and that you need not carry a balance; CFPB says paying in full every month is the best approach. Widely repeated by secondary sites but not confirmable at a primary source — either drop the table row or label it explicitly as an unconfirmed community observation.

facts.claim: Blog text: a credit limit increase lowers utilization without paying anything, and many issuers grant one with a soft pull.
facts.source: The arithmetic is trivially true (raising the denominator lowers the fraction), but no federal regulator or scoring model publishes whether issuers use soft or hard pulls for limit-increase requests — it varies by issuer and is not a rule anyone sets. The blog already tells readers to ask their issuer, which is the correct handling; keep that caveat.

facts.claim: An emergency fund is a cash reserve covering three to six months of essential expenses (manifest gloss; Stage 1 Module 08 'Tier 3 — The Emergency Fund: 3–6 Months of Expenses'; Stage 4 'Roughly: three to six months of expenses').
facts.corrected_to: The 3–6 month range is Ramsey Solutions' Baby Step 3 ('3–6 months of expenses in a fully funded emergency fund'), not a government standard — and it is the LOW end of federal guidance. FDIC consumer guidance says 'at least six months of living expenses in a federally insured product.' SEC Investor.gov says 'up to six months of their income.' CFPB deliberately sets no number: 'The amount you need to have in an emergency savings fund depends on your situation.' The page should present 3–6 months as a widely used convention with a named origin, note that FDIC and SEC both anchor at six, and note that CFPB declines to set a universal target.
facts.source: Ramsey Solutions, 7 Baby Steps (original author's own definition); FDIC Consumer Resource Center, 'Saving for the Unexpected and Your Future' (Jan 2025); SEC Investor.gov, 'Save for a Rainy Day'; CFPB, 'An essential guide to building an emergency fund'

facts.claim: Stage 1 Module 08: 'For employees with stable income: aim for 3 months of essential expenses. For gig workers, freelancers, or single-income households: aim for 6 months minimum.'
facts.corrected_to: No primary source sets this employment-type split. The FDIC's published figure ('at least six months of living expenses') carries no stable-employment carve-out, so the 3-month tier for salaried workers is below the only federal number available. BLS data supports sizing by job-search risk rather than job type: median duration of unemployment was 10.5 weeks (~2.4 months) in July 2026, but 1.8 million people — 25.5% of all unemployed — had been jobless 27 weeks or more, so a 3-month fund covers the median case and fails the quarter of cases that run long.
facts.source: FDIC Consumer Resource Center, 'Saving for the Unexpected and Your Future'; BLS Employment Situation, July 2026 (released 2026-08-07); FRED series UEMPMED (BLS median duration of unemployment)

facts.claim: Stage 2 Module 01 targets a '$1,000 emergency fund' as the first real milestone, presented without attribution.
facts.corrected_to: $1,000 is Ramsey Solutions' Baby Step 1 verbatim — 'Save $1,000 for your starter emergency fund.' It is a named commercial program's figure, not a federal or regulatory benchmark, and the glossary page should attribute it. No government body publishes a starter-fund dollar target; CFPB's position is that 'even a small amount can provide some financial security.'
facts.source: Ramsey Solutions, 7 Baby Steps; CFPB, 'An essential guide to building an emergency fund'

facts.claim: Stage 1 Module 08: 'Tier 1 — The Micro Buffer: $100 to $500.'
facts.corrected_to: No primary source sets a $100–$500 threshold; it is a house convention. It is directionally consistent with CFPB guidance that building savings 'of any size' is valuable and that 'even a small amount can provide some financial security,' but the specific range is not a published figure and should not be presented as one.
facts.source: CFPB, 'An essential guide to building an emergency fund'

facts.claim: Emergency savings belong in an FDIC-insured deposit account, and that insurance covers $250,000.
facts.corrected_to: Standard FDIC deposit insurance is $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, for each account ownership category. Coverage is automatic on opening a deposit account at an insured bank.
facts.source: FDIC, Deposit Insurance resource page

facts.claim: The same $250,000 protection applies at a credit union (relevant because Stage 1 Module 09 routes readers to credit unions).
facts.corrected_to: NCUA Share Insurance Fund covers $250,000 per member, per insured credit union, per ownership category — identical limit and structure to FDIC.
facts.source: NCUA, Share Insurance Coverage

facts.claim: Most Americans could handle a $400 emergency expense — the standard framing statistic for why an emergency fund matters.
facts.corrected_to: 63% of adults said they would cover a hypothetical $400 emergency expense entirely using cash or its equivalent (cash, savings, or a credit card paid off at the next statement) — meaning 37% could not. Unchanged from prior years. From the 2025 SHED, fielded 17–28 October 2025, published 19 May 2026.
facts.source: Federal Reserve, Report on the Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025 (SHED), Executive Summary and Savings and Investments section

facts.claim: Most people do not have three months of expenses saved (the core statistic a page on this term needs).
facts.corrected_to: 55% of adults said they had set aside money to cover three months of expenses in 2025 — unchanged from 2024, down from 59% in 2021. 30% of adults said they could not cover three months of expenses by ANY means (savings, borrowing, or selling assets).
facts.source: Federal Reserve, Report on the Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025 (SHED), Savings and Investments section

facts.claim: Stage 1 Module 09: a payday loan gives you $300 and charges $345–400 in two weeks, 'That is a 400% annual interest rate' (echoed in Stage 4 as 'a 400% loan').
facts.corrected_to: The APR is right; the top of the dollar range is too high. CFPB: a typical two-week payday loan carries a $15 per $100 fee, which 'equates to an annual percentage rate (APR) of almost 400 percent' — CFPB research puts the median at 391% APR on a 14-day loan. On $300 that is a $45 fee, so $345 is correct. $400 implies roughly $33 per $100, above the $10–$30 per $100 range CFPB cites for state fee caps. Use '$345, roughly a 400% APR' rather than a $345–400 range.
facts.source: CFPB, 'What is a payday loan?' (Ask CFPB); CFPB, 'Highlights from CFPB Research: Payday Loans'

facts.claim: Stage 1 Module 09: 'The average borrower takes out 8 loans per year.'
facts.corrected_to: 10, not 8. CFPB's payday lending factsheet reports a median of 10 transactions by borrowers over 12 months, a median storefront loan size of $350, median fees of $15 per $100 on a typical 14-day loan, $458 in fees over the course of a year, and nearly 200 days per year in debt. 14% of borrowers take 20 or more loans annually. Note this is a median, not an average — the course says 'average.'
facts.source: CFPB, Payday Loans factsheet (April 2013) and CFPB Data Point: Payday Lending (March 2014)

facts.claim: A high-yield savings account (HYSA) pays meaningfully more than an ordinary savings account, so an emergency fund should sit in one (Stage 1 Module 08, Stage 2 Module 01).
facts.corrected_to: The gap is real and large, and can be stated from primary data without quoting any bank's rate: the FDIC national deposit rate for savings was 0.38% in July 2026, while the FOMC's federal funds target range is 3.50–3.75% (set 11 December 2025). Individual HYSA APYs are bank-specific and set by no public body — do not publish a specific '4%' style figure as a verified number; cite the 0.38% national average and the fed funds range as the bracket.
facts.source: FDIC National Rates and Rate Caps via FRED series SNDR (July 2026); Federal Reserve, Open Market Operations / FOMC target range

facts.claim: Cash held in an emergency fund loses purchasing power to inflation (Stage 4: 'you are paying a small, certain cost every year, in lost purchasing power').
facts.corrected_to: Correct and quantifiable as of the latest print: CPI-U rose 3.5% over the 12 months ending June 2026 (core, all items less food and energy, +2.6%), against a 0.38% national average savings rate — so an ordinary savings account lost roughly 3.1 percentage points of purchasing power over the year. Released 14 July 2026; the July CPI print was not yet out as of 11 August 2026.
facts.source: BLS, Consumer Price Index news release, June 2026; FDIC National Rate: Savings via FRED (SNDR)

facts.claim: Americans are saving too little to build a fund quickly (context for the Stage 2 '30-day sprint' framing).
facts.corrected_to: The personal saving rate was 2.7% of disposable personal income in June 2026 (BEA, released 30 July 2026). At that rate a household would need years, not a 30-day sprint, to reach a 3-month fund from savings alone — which is the honest case for the course's sell-things-and-pick-up-hours approach.
facts.source: BEA, Personal Saving Rate

facts.claim: Interest earned on an emergency fund in a savings account is taxable.
facts.corrected_to: Yes. A payer must issue Form 1099-INT at $10 or more of interest, but the IRS is explicit that the obligation does not depend on the form: 'You must report all taxable and tax-exempt interest on your federal income tax return, even if you don't receive a Form 1099-INT or Form 1099-OID.' Interest on bank accounts, money market accounts and CDs is taxable interest.
facts.source: IRS, Topic no. 403, Interest received

facts.claim: Raiding a retirement account instead of holding an emergency fund is expensive (Stage 4: 'income tax on the whole balance plus a 10% early-withdrawal penalty under 59½').
facts.corrected_to: Correct: a 10% additional tax on early distributions applies to withdrawals before age 59½, on top of ordinary income tax, unless an exception applies. Exceptions relevant to an emergency-fund page include separation from service at age 55+, unreimbursed medical expenses above 7.5% of AGI, health insurance premiums while unemployed, disability, and up to $5,000 per child for birth or adoption.
facts.source: IRS, Retirement topics — Tax on early distributions

facts.claim: Stage 1 Module 09 and Stage 2 direct readers to call 211 as the alternative when there is no emergency fund.
facts.corrected_to: 211 was assigned by the FCC as a national abbreviated dialing code for access to community information and referral services, in the Third Report and Order released 31 July 2000. It is a nationwide assignment; actual service availability is delivered by local providers.
facts.source: FCC Third Report and Order, FCC 00-256 (released 2000-07-31); FCC consumer guide, 'Dial 211 for Essential Community Services'
