facts.claim: Inflation rate is computed as (price index now − price index a year ago) ÷ price index a year ago × 100, reported year-over-year.
facts.source: BLS, Consumer Price Index News Release, June 2026 (12-month percent changes, not seasonally adjusted) — https://www.bls.gov/news.release/cpi.nr0.htm

facts.claim: CPI is published by the Bureau of Labor Statistics; the PCE price index is published by the Bureau of Economic Analysis as part of the Personal Income and Outlays report.
facts.source: BLS CPI news release https://www.bls.gov/news.release/cpi.nr0.htm and BEA, Personal Income and Outlays, June 2026 https://www.bea.gov/news/2026/personal-income-and-outlays-june-2026

facts.claim: The Federal Reserve's longer-run inflation objective is 2 percent as measured by the annual change in the price index for personal consumption expenditures (headline PCE, not core, and not CPI).
facts.source: FOMC, Statement on Longer-Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy — adopted effective January 24, 2012, as reaffirmed effective January 27, 2026 — https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/files/fomc_longerrungoals.pdf

facts.claim: The Fed still frames its 2% goal as 'average inflation of 2 percent over time' with a makeup strategy, and pledges to respond to 'shortfalls' of employment.
facts.corrected_to: The current Statement on Longer-Run Goals contains neither phrase. The August 22, 2025 framework revision removed flexible average inflation targeting and the 'shortfalls' language; the 2 percent PCE goal itself was explicitly not part of that review. The statement now says the Committee will 'act forcefully to ensure that longer-term inflation expectations remain well anchored.' Any glossary copy describing the Fed as an average-inflation targeter is stale by roughly a year.
facts.source: FOMC Statement on Longer-Run Goals (reaffirmed 2026-01-27) https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/files/fomc_longerrungoals.pdf ; Federal Reserve press release, August 22, 2025 https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20250822a.htm

facts.claim: Course text (EconomicsCourse stage 2, Module 02 table): shelter is '~33–35%' of the CPI and 'around a third of the total index'.
facts.corrected_to: 35.625% of CPI-U (December 2025 relative importance, 2024 expenditure weights). The June 2026 news release shows 35.149% on May 2026 relative importance. Shelter is meaningfully more than a third; the course band's top end sits below the actual figure.
facts.source: BLS, Relative importance of components in the CPI, U.S. city average, December 2025 (Table 1, 2024 Weights) — https://www.bls.gov/cpi/tables/relative-importance/2025.htm

facts.claim: Within the CPI, owners' equivalent rent of residences is 26.204% of all items and rent of primary residence is 7.840%; the whole Housing group is 44.469%.
facts.source: BLS, Relative importance of CPI components, December 2025 — https://www.bls.gov/cpi/tables/relative-importance/2025.htm

facts.claim: Course text: food ~13%, transportation ~16%, medical care ~8%, energy ~7% of the CPI.
facts.corrected_to: Exact December 2025 relative importance: Food 13.698%, Transportation 16.316%, Medical care 8.423%, Energy 6.383%. Energy's relative importance drifts up during the year with energy prices — the June 2026 release shows 7.791% on May 2026 weights — so the course's ~7% is inside the observed range. Use the exact figures on the glossary page.
facts.source: BLS, Relative importance of CPI components, December 2025 https://www.bls.gov/cpi/tables/relative-importance/2025.htm ; BLS CPI Table 1, June 2026 https://www.bls.gov/news.release/cpi.t01.htm

facts.claim: Course text: 'CPI weights are updated on a fixed schedule and held constant in between' / 'Periodic, fixed in between' / 'updated periodically'.
facts.corrected_to: Since January 2023 BLS updates CPI spending weights ANNUALLY, using a single calendar year of Consumer Expenditure Survey data with a two-year lag (2021 spending → 2023 indexes; 2023 spending → 2025 indexes; the December 2025 table is labelled '2024 Weights'). Before 2023 the update was biennial and used two years of CE data. 'Periodic' is vague enough to read as the pre-2023 regime.
facts.source: BLS, Relative Importance and Weight Information for the Consumer Price Indexes https://www.bls.gov/cpi/tables/relative-importance/home.htm ; BLS, Comparison of 2025 CPI data using new weights and previous weights https://www.bls.gov/cpi/tables/relative-importance/weight-update-comparison-2025.htm

facts.claim: Course text: 'CPI is used to index Social Security'.
facts.corrected_to: The Social Security COLA is set on the CPI-W (Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers), NOT the headline CPI-U that the media quotes, comparing the third-quarter average to the third-quarter average of the last year a COLA took effect. The 2026 COLA is 2.8%. CPI-W covers about 30% of the U.S. population; CPI-U covers over 90%.
facts.source: SSA, Latest Cost-of-Living Adjustment https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/latestCOLA.html ; BLS CPI Questions and Answers https://www.bls.gov/cpi/questions-and-answers.htm

facts.claim: TIPS are indexed to the CPI.
facts.corrected_to: Specifically the non-seasonally adjusted CPI-U, with a three-month lag: 'The Ref CPI for the first day of any calendar month is the CPI for the third preceding calendar month.'
facts.source: 31 CFR Part 356, Appendix B (Uniform Offering Circular, Formulas and Examples for Inflation-Protected Securities) — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/subtitle-B/chapter-II/subchapter-A/part-356/appendix-Appendix%20B%20to%20Part%20356

facts.claim: CPI-U measures the spending of a 'typical urban household'.
facts.corrected_to: BLS wording: 'The CPI-U population constitutes over 90 percent of the U.S. population and covers households in all areas of the United States.' Use 'over 90 percent', not the older '87%' or '93%' figures still circulating on secondary sites.
facts.source: BLS, Consumer Price Index Frequently Asked Questions — https://www.bls.gov/cpi/questions-and-answers.htm

facts.claim: Course text: owners' equivalent rent is used for 'the roughly two thirds of households that own their home'.
facts.corrected_to: The U.S. homeownership rate is 65.0% (±0.5), second quarter 2026, unchanged from Q2 2025. 'Roughly two thirds' is a fair rounding of 65.0%; give the exact figure with its as-of date on the glossary page.
facts.source: U.S. Census Bureau, Quarterly Residential Vacancies and Homeownership, Second Quarter 2026, released July 28, 2026 — https://www.census.gov/housing/hvs/files/currenthvspress.pdf

facts.claim: Latest published U.S. CPI reading a 2026 reader needs.
facts.corrected_to: June 2026 CPI, released July 14, 2026: all items +3.5% over 12 months (NSA); all items less food and energy +2.6%; shelter +3.3%; energy +15.7%. NOTE FOR PUBLISHING: the July 2026 CPI is scheduled for Wednesday, August 12, 2026 at 8:30 a.m. ET — one day after today. Any hard number baked into the page will be stale within 24 hours; use the live market-data feed or a dated 'as of' line.
facts.source: BLS, Consumer Price Index — June 2026 (USDL-26-1191) https://www.bls.gov/news.release/cpi.nr0.htm and Table 1 https://www.bls.gov/news.release/cpi.t01.htm

facts.claim: Latest published U.S. PCE reading a 2026 reader needs.
facts.corrected_to: June 2026 PCE, released July 30, 2026: headline PCE price index +3.7% from one year ago; PCE excluding food and energy (core PCE) +3.3% from one year ago.
facts.source: BEA, Personal Income and Outlays, June 2026 — https://www.bea.gov/news/2026/personal-income-and-outlays-june-2026

facts.claim: Course text: PCE's continuously-updating weights 'generally makes PCE run slightly below CPI'.
facts.corrected_to: Not true in the current data and should not be stated as a standing rule. On the June 2026 releases PCE is ABOVE CPI: headline 3.7% vs 3.5%, and core PCE 3.3% vs core CPI 2.6% — a 0.7 percentage point gap in the opposite direction from the one the course describes. BEA itself names four effects (formula, weight, scope, other) and asserts no general direction. Write the mechanism, not a direction.
facts.source: BEA, Personal Income and Outlays, June 2026 https://www.bea.gov/news/2026/personal-income-and-outlays-june-2026 ; BLS CPI June 2026 https://www.bls.gov/news.release/cpi.nr0.htm ; BEA FAQ 555 https://www.bea.gov/help/faq/555

facts.claim: CPI and PCE diverge because of differences in scope, weights and index formula.
facts.corrected_to: BEA names four effects precisely: FORMULA effect (PCE uses the Fisher-Ideal formula, CPI a modified Laspeyres); WEIGHT effect; SCOPE effect ('PCE measures spending by and on behalf of the personal sector, which includes both households and nonprofit institutions serving households; the CPI measures out-of-pocket spending by households'); and OTHER effects (seasonal adjustment, price and residual differences). The course omits the fourth.
facts.source: BEA, 'What accounts for the differences in the PCE price index and the Consumer Price Index?' FAQ 555 — https://www.bea.gov/help/faq/555

facts.claim: Shelter has a larger weight in CPI than in PCE; medical care has a larger weight in PCE because PCE includes care paid for on households' behalf.
facts.source: BLS, 'Differences between the Consumer Price Index and the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index', Beyond the Numbers, May 2011 — https://www.bls.gov/opub/btn/archive/differences-between-the-consumer-price-index-and-the-personal-consumption-expenditures-price-index.pdf

facts.claim: CPI is released earlier in the month than PCE.
facts.corrected_to: Confirmed by the June 2026 reference month: CPI released July 14, 2026; PCE released July 30, 2026 — a 16-day gap.
facts.source: BLS https://www.bls.gov/news.release/cpi.nr0.htm ; BEA https://www.bea.gov/news/2026/personal-income-and-outlays-june-2026

facts.claim: There is a hole in the U.S. CPI series: October and November 2025.
facts.corrected_to: BLS did not collect CPI data from October 1, 2025 through November 12, 2025 because of the lapse in appropriations. 'Missing CPI data affected October and November 2025 indexes.' The effect also propagated forward: 'Missing October 2025 data also affected April 2026 rent and owner's equivalent rent indexes.' The Cleveland Fed had to interpolate October 2025 to keep median and trimmed-mean CPI running. THE COURSE DOES NOT MENTION THIS AT ALL, and it matters directly to the course's own Module 01 teaching on year-over-year base effects — any 12-month comparison spanning that window rests on non-collected data.
facts.source: BLS, '2025 Federal Government Shutdown Impact on Consumer Expenditure Surveys (CE) and Consumer Price Index (CPI)' https://www.bls.gov/cpi/additional-resources/2025-federal-government-shutdown-impact-cpi.htm ; Cleveland Fed Median CPI https://www.clevelandfed.org/indicators-and-data/median-cpi

facts.claim: Core inflation excludes food and energy.
facts.corrected_to: BLS publishes it as 'all items less food and energy'; BEA as 'PCE price index excluding food and energy'. 'Core' is the market shorthand, not the agency label.
facts.source: BLS CPI Table 1 https://www.bls.gov/news.release/cpi.t01.htm ; BEA Personal Income and Outlays, June 2026 https://www.bea.gov/news/2026/personal-income-and-outlays-june-2026

facts.claim: 'Supercore' means core services excluding shelter/housing, and the concept traces to Fed Chair Jerome Powell.
facts.corrected_to: The three-way decomposition — 'core goods inflation, housing services inflation, and inflation in core services other than housing' — is from Chair Jerome H. Powell, 'Inflation and the Labor Market', Hutchins Center on Fiscal and Monetary Policy, Brookings Institution, Washington D.C., November 30, 2022. Powell does NOT use the word 'supercore' anywhere in that speech; it is market shorthand applied afterward. The course already flags it as 'informally called supercore' — that framing is correct and should be preserved verbatim on the glossary page.
facts.source: Federal Reserve, Speech by Chair Powell on inflation and the labor market, November 30, 2022 — https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/speech/powell20221130a.htm

facts.claim: Median CPI and trimmed-mean CPI are alternative core measures published by the Cleveland Fed.
facts.corrected_to: Cleveland Fed definitions: median CPI is 'the one-month inflation rate of the component whose expenditure weight is in the 50th percentile of price changes'; the 16% trimmed-mean CPI is 'a weighted average of one-month inflation rates of components whose expenditure weights fall below the 92nd percentile and above the 8th percentile of price changes'. Latest (June 2026): median CPI 2.7% and 16% trimmed-mean CPI 2.6% over 12 months — both below headline CPI at 3.5%, consistent with a narrow, energy-led print.
facts.source: Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland, Median CPI — https://www.clevelandfed.org/indicators-and-data/median-cpi

facts.claim: Sticky-price CPI tracks only categories whose prices change infrequently.
facts.corrected_to: Confirmed as a concept and as a live series: the Atlanta Fed sorts CPI components 'based on the frequency of their price adjustment', and the sticky-price CPI rose 2.8% over 12 months in June 2026. The specific numeric cutoff separating sticky from flexible components is not stated on the Atlanta Fed's public pages — do not put a threshold number on the glossary page.
facts.source: Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, Sticky-Price CPI https://www.atlantafed.org/research-and-data/data/sticky-price-cpi and explainer https://www.atlantafed.org/research-and-data/data/sticky-price-cpi/explainer

facts.claim: Breakeven inflation = nominal Treasury yield − TIPS yield at the same maturity.
facts.corrected_to: Confirmed as the construction of the published series: FRED's 10-Year Breakeven Inflation Rate (T10YIE) is DGS10 minus DFII10. Latest value 2.29% on August 10, 2026.
facts.source: FRED, 10-Year Breakeven Inflation Rate (T10YIE), Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis — https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/T10YIE

facts.claim: The 5y5y forward breakeven measures expected average inflation for the five years beginning five years from now, and is the cleanest read on whether expectations are anchored.
facts.corrected_to: Definition confirmed: FRED T5YIFR measures 'expected inflation (on average) over the five-year period that begins five years from today', derived from 10-year and 5-year nominal and inflation-indexed Treasury yields. Latest value 2.33% on August 10, 2026 — i.e. essentially at the Fed's 2% PCE goal (breakevens are CPI-referenced, so they sit structurally above a PCE target) while spot CPI runs 3.5%. Expectations are anchored on this measure as of today.
facts.source: FRED, 5-Year, 5-Year Forward Inflation Expectation Rate (T5YIFR), Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis — https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/T5YIFR

facts.claim: The New York Fed's consumer expectations survey is one of the survey-based measures of inflation expectations.
facts.corrected_to: The Survey of Consumer Expectations is run monthly by the New York Fed's Center for Microeconomic Data on a rotating panel of roughly 1,300 household heads. Median one-year-ahead inflation expectation was 3.6% in the July 2026 survey, released August 7, 2026 — well above the 2.29% ten-year market breakeven, the classic households-above-markets gap.
facts.source: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Survey of Consumer Expectations — https://www.newyorkfed.org/microeconomics/sce

facts.claim: The real interest rate, not the nominal policy rate, determines whether policy is tight or loose — worth a live example.
facts.corrected_to: Current values for a worked example: federal funds target range 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent and interest on reserve balances 3.65%, both effective July 30, 2026; headline PCE inflation 3.7%; 10-year TIPS real yield 2.40% (August 7, 2026). On the course's own subtraction convention the real policy rate is approximately zero (3.625% midpoint − 3.7% inflation), i.e. neither restrictive nor stimulative — a live illustration of exactly the Module 07 point.
facts.source: Federal Reserve, Implementation Note issued July 29, 2026 https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20260729a1.htm ; BEA https://www.bea.gov/news/2026/personal-income-and-outlays-june-2026 ; FRED DFII10 https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DFII10

facts.claim: Course text: 'The euro area's HICP excludes owners' equivalent rent entirely', making euro-area and U.S. inflation non-comparable during a housing cycle.
facts.corrected_to: Confirmed, with the precise mechanism: owner-occupied housing costs are outside the HICP. A 2018 European Commission report 'assessed that the OOHPI was not suitable for integration into the coverage of the HICP', and it remains outside as of April 2026 despite an ECB recommendation to include it. Eurostat publishes a separate Owner-Occupied Housing Price Index on a net-acquisitions basis — a different concept from the CPI's rental-equivalence approach, not merely a different weight.
facts.source: Eurostat, Statistics Explained: Housing price statistics — owner-occupied housing price index — https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Housing_price_statistics_-_owner-occupied_housing_price_index

facts.claim: Course text, Module 07: 'Earn 6% nominal with 4% inflation and a 25% tax rate: you pay 1.5% in tax, leaving 4.5% nominal and just 0.5% real. The effective tax rate on your actual gain was 75%, not 25%.'
facts.corrected_to: Arithmetic is internally consistent on the subtraction (approximate) convention the course uses: tax = 0.25 × 6% = 1.5%; after-tax nominal 4.5%; real 4.5% − 4% = 0.5%; 1.5 ÷ 2.0 = 75%. Under the exact Fisher formula the module itself states earlier — (1+nominal)÷(1+inflation)−1 — the pre-tax real gain is 1.923% and the effective rate on the real gain is 78%, and the after-tax real return is 0.481%. Both are defensible; the page should say which convention it is using rather than mixing the exact formula and the subtraction shortcut on the same page as the course does.
facts.source: Arithmetic verification of the course example against the exact Fisher relation stated in the same module (EconomicsCourse stage 2, Module 07)

facts.claim: Deflation forces the real interest rate up even with the policy rate at zero, because nominal rates cannot fall far below zero.
facts.corrected_to: The mechanism follows directly from the confirmed Fisher relation (real = nominal − inflation), so it is arithmetically sound, but it is a theoretical proposition rather than a published figure and no primary body 'sets' it. Present it as reasoning, not as a sourced fact. facts.claim: The Relative Strength Index was created by J. Welles Wilder Jr.
facts.source: Primary: the work itself. Internet Archive scan of Wilder, J. Welles Jr., 'New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems' (Trend Research, Greensboro NC, 1978, ISBN 0-89459-027-8) — title page/copyright 1978 and table of contents listing Section VI 'The Relative Strength Index'. Corroborated by Wilder's own signed article, 'The Relative Strength Index', Technical Analysis of STOCKS & COMMODITIES V.4:9, pp.343-346.

facts.claim: Course text (TA Stage 4, Module 02): 'The Relative Strength Index, or RSI, was introduced by J. Welles Wilder in a 1978 magazine article.'
facts.corrected_to: Cite the book, not a magazine article: Wilder introduced RSI in his 1978 book 'New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems' (Trend Research, Greensboro NC; ISBN 0-89459-027-8), where it is Section VI. The frequently repeated claim of a June 1978 Commodities magazine article could not be confirmed against any primary source — no issue, page range or archival record was reachable. Wilder's own bylined magazine treatment of RSI that IS documented is a later one: Technical Analysis of STOCKS & COMMODITIES, Vol. 4 Issue 9, pp.343-346, December 1986. The 1978 book is the safe, verifiable citation.
facts.source: Internet Archive catalogue record and scan of the 1978 Trend Research edition (archive.org/details/newconceptsintec00wild); TradingView official RSI documentation, which also attributes RSI to the 1978 book; store.traders.com product record for the 1986 S&C article.

facts.claim: RSI oscillates on a fixed scale from 0 to 100.
facts.source: Deductive from the defining formula RSI = 100 - 100/(1+RS) with RS >= 0, which bounds the output to [0,100]. Independently stated in Schwab/thinkorswim Learning Center RSI study reference ('rates the strength of a security on a scale from 0 to 100') and TradingView official docs ('RSI operates between a scale of 0 and 100').

facts.claim: Wilder's original rule: RSI above 70 signals overbought/tops, RSI below 30 signals oversold/bottoms.
facts.source: Primary: Wilder, J. Welles Jr., 'The Relative Strength Index', Technical Analysis of STOCKS & COMMODITIES V.4:9 (Dec 1986), pp.343-346 — the publisher's abstract of Wilder's own article states tops and bottoms are indicated when RSI exceeds 70 or drops below 30. Corroborated by TradingView official docs and by Schwab/thinkorswim, whose RSI study ships default levels of 70 and 30.

facts.claim: The RSI formula is RSI = 100 - 100/(1 + RS), where RS = average gain over the lookback / average loss over the lookback.
facts.source: TradingView official RSI documentation gives 'RSI = 100 - 100/(1 + RS); RS = Average Gain of n days UP / Average Loss of n days DOWN'; StockCharts ChartSchool gives the identical pair. NOTE ON PRIMACY: Wilder's own Section VI text was NOT reachable — the unrestricted archive.org scan truncates mid-Section V, the 1978 lending copy is access-restricted, and Wilder's 1986 S&C article is paywalled ($4.95). Two independent normative implementations state it identically, so state it with attribution to Wilder's 1978 book.

facts.claim: The lookback period is 14, and 14 remains the default on essentially every charting platform.
facts.source: TradingView official RSI documentation: '14 bars is the default.' StockCharts ChartSchool: default 14 periods. Verified as the platform default as of today.

facts.claim: Wilder himself chose 14 days as the averaging period.
facts.source: Wilder's Section VI text could not be read (archive.org unrestricted copy truncates before Section VI; the 1978 lending copy at archive.org/details/newconceptsintec00wild is access-restricted; the 1986 S&C article is paywalled). Universally restated but not primary-confirmed here. Safe phrasing: 'the 14-period default that has been standard since Wilder's work', not 'Wilder used 14 days' as a sourced quotation.

facts.claim: Wilder's own published list of RSI uses includes: tops and bottoms at 70/30, chart formations that appear on the RSI line but not on the bar chart, failure swings, support and resistance that shows on RSI more clearly than on price, and divergence between RSI and price signalling turning points.
facts.source: Primary: publisher's abstract of Wilder's own article, 'The Relative Strength Index', Technical Analysis of STOCKS & COMMODITIES V.4:9 (Dec 1986), pp.343-346, store.traders.com. This confirms the course's claims that RSI forms chart-pattern-like shapes, that traders read trendlines/support-resistance on the RSI line, and that divergence is an original Wilder use. GAP: 'failure swing' is one of Wilder's five original uses and the course passage never names it — the glossary page should.

facts.claim: Divergence — price making a higher high while RSI makes a lower high — is a recognised RSI reversal warning that originates with Wilder.
facts.source: Primary: same Wilder 1986 S&C article abstract, which lists 'divergence between RSI and price action signalling potential turning points'. This confirms attribution and definition only. It is NOT a confirmation that divergence predicts reversals — no primary source establishes a hit rate, so the page must not imply one.

facts.claim: Course table: 'Chuck LeBeau — overbought 75, oversold 25.'
facts.source: No primary source found. The primary would be LeBeau & Lucas, 'Technical Traders Guide to Computer Analysis of the Futures Markets' (Irwin, 1992, ISBN 1-55623-468-6); it is not on the Internet Archive (advanced-search returned 0 records) and no reachable text attributes 75/25 to LeBeau. StockCharts ChartSchool's RSI page does not mention LeBeau at all. Recommend dropping the named attribution or labelling it 'commonly cited' rather than sourced.

facts.claim: Course table: 'Constance Brown — uptrend 90/40, downtrend 60/10.'
facts.corrected_to: Two authoritative secondary sources disagree on Brown's numbers. StockCharts ChartSchool: 'RSI tends to fluctuate between 40 and 90 in a bull market (uptrend) with the 40-50 zone acting as support' and 'between 10 and 60 in a bear market (downtrend) with the 50-60 zone acting as resistance' — this matches the course table. CMT Association (the technical-analysis professional body), 'Mastering the Relative Strength Index', 9 May 2025: 'In an uptrend, RSI operates in a bullish range with lows near 40-50 and highs between 80-90. In a downtrend, RSI stays in a bearish range with lows around 20-30 and highs limited to 55-65.' The primary source, Brown, 'Technical Analysis for the Trading Professional' (McGraw-Hill, 1999, ISBN 0-07-012062-5), is access-restricted on the Internet Archive and could not be read. Do not print 90/40 and 60/10 as hard figures; either attribute the exact rendering to StockCharts or describe the idea qualitatively (RSI ranges shift upward in uptrends and downward in downtrends).
facts.source: StockCharts ChartSchool RSI page vs CMT Association ChartAdvisor RSI article (2025-05-09); primary Brown 1999 unreachable (archive.org item technicalanalysi00brow, access-restricted-item: true).

facts.claim: Course text: 'Some analysts even trade the opposite: buying strength when RSI pushes past 75 in an uptrend.'
facts.corrected_to: No named source and no primary source for the number 75. The named practitioner behind this school of thought is Andrew Cardwell, whom StockCharts ChartSchool credits with 'positive and negative reversals for RSI' and with reinterpreting divergences as bull/bear-market phenomena — the opposite of Wilder's original framework. If the page keeps this idea, attribute it to Cardwell and drop the unsourced 75 threshold.
facts.source: StockCharts ChartSchool RSI page (Cardwell attribution). No primary Cardwell publication reachable.

facts.claim: RSI measures a security against its own price history, not against other stocks or an index (i.e. it is not comparative 'relative strength').
facts.source: Follows directly from the formula, which takes only that security's own up-closes and down-closes as inputs (TradingView official docs; StockCharts ChartSchool). This is a genuine and common point of confusion and is worth keeping prominent on the glossary page.

facts.claim: RSI's midpoint is 50, and readings above 50 indicate an uptrend while readings below 50 indicate a downtrend.
facts.source: 50 as the arithmetic midpoint of a 0-100 scale is trivially true. The trend-direction interpretation is a widely used convention with no primary source establishing it as Wilder's rule and no primary source establishing predictive accuracy; Wilder's own published list of RSI uses (S&C V.4:9) does not include a 50-line trend filter. Present it as a common convention, not as Wilder's rule or as an established statistical fact.

facts.claim: Stochastic's traditional overbought/oversold levels are 80 and 20, tighter than RSI's 70/30 (comparison stated inside the RSI passage).
facts.source: The RSI half (70/30) is confirmed via Wilder's 1986 S&C article abstract and thinkorswim defaults. The stochastic half (80/20) was not verified against its primary source, George C. Lane, in this pass — it belongs to the stochastic-oscillator glossary entry and should be fact-checked there before the RSI page asserts it.

facts.claim: There is no annually-updated figure on this term.
facts.source: RSI is a fixed mathematical construct: the formula, the 0-100 range, the 14 default and the 70/30 levels have not changed since 1978. Nothing on this page needs a 2026 refresh; the only values that could drift are platform defaults, verified current as of today against TradingView and Schwab/thinkorswim documentation.

facts.claim: The 2026 IRA contribution limit is $7,500, and it is a combined cap across all of a person's traditional and Roth IRAs, not per account.
facts.source: IRS IR-2025-111 (Nov 13, 2025) and IRS Notice 2025-67 (section 219(b)(5)(A)); IRS 'Retirement topics - IRA contribution limits' confirms the combined-cap wording: 'the total contributions you make each year to all of your traditional IRAs and Roth IRAs can't be more than' the limit. Course text (FL Stage 3, Module 10) states $7,500 — correct.

facts.claim: The 2026 IRA catch-up contribution for people age 50 and over is $1,100, for a total of $8,600.
facts.source: IRS IR-2025-111: catch-up 'increased to $1,100, up from $1,000 for 2025'; Notice 2025-67, section 219(b)(5)(B)(ii). Course states $1,100 (Module 10) and $8,600 for 50+ (Module 11) — both correct.

facts.claim: For 2026 the Roth IRA contribution phase-out range is $153,000-$168,000 of MAGI for single and head-of-household filers.
facts.source: IRS IR-2025-111 (Nov 13, 2025); IRS Notice 2025-67, section 408A(c)(3)(A)(ii). Course states $153,000-$168,000 — correct.

facts.claim: For 2026 the Roth IRA contribution phase-out range is $242,000-$252,000 of MAGI for married filing jointly.
facts.source: IRS IR-2025-111 (Nov 13, 2025); IRS Notice 2025-67. Course states $242,000-$252,000 — correct.

facts.claim: For married filing separately (living with spouse), the 2026 Roth phase-out range is $0-$10,000 — effectively no direct Roth contribution.
facts.source: IRS IR-2025-111; IRS Notice 2025-67 ('remains $0 to $10,000'). NOTE: the course omits this filing status entirely — the glossary page should state it.

facts.claim: A Roth IRA contribution cannot exceed the person's taxable compensation for the year, and there is no upper age limit on contributing.
facts.source: IRS 'Retirement topics - IRA contribution limits': limit is '$7,500 ... or if less, your taxable compensation for the year'; 'For 2020 and later, there is no age limit on making regular contributions to traditional or Roth IRAs.' Supports the course's custodial-Roth-for-a-working-teen point (Stage 5, Module 11).

facts.claim: A contribution for a tax year can be made up to the due date of that year's return, not including extensions — so 15 April 2027 for the 2026 tax year.
facts.source: IRS Publication 590-A: 'Contributions can be made to your traditional IRA for a year at any time during the year or by the due date for filing your return for that year, not including extensions.' Same rule applies to Roth IRAs.

facts.claim: Roth IRA contributions are never deductible, and qualified distributions are tax-free.
facts.source: IRS 'Roth IRAs' topic page: 'You cannot deduct contributions to a Roth IRA' and 'If you satisfy the requirements, qualified distributions are tax-free.'

facts.claim: Roth IRA distributions follow a fixed ordering: regular contributions come out first, then conversions, then earnings.
facts.source: IRS Publication 590-B, 'Ordering Rules for Distributions' — regular contributions first, then conversion and rollover contributions, then earnings. This is the mechanism behind the course's central Module 10 claim.

facts.claim: You can withdraw your own Roth contributions at any age, for any reason, with no tax and no 10% penalty; the 10% additional tax applies only to amounts includible in gross income (i.e. earnings).
facts.source: IRS Tax Topic 557: 'The 10% additional tax applies to the part of the distribution that you have to include in gross income. It's in addition to any regular income tax on that amount.' Combined with the Pub 590-B ordering rules, contributions come out first and are not includible. Course claim verified.

facts.claim: A qualified (fully tax-free) Roth distribution requires the 5-year period plus one of four conditions: age 59-1/2, death, disability, or first-time home purchase.
facts.source: IRS Publication 590-B, 'What Are Qualified Distributions?' — 5-year period beginning with the first tax year a contribution was made, plus one of the four listed conditions.

facts.claim: The first-time homebuyer exception is capped at $10,000 over a lifetime.
facts.source: IRS Publication 590-B ($10,000 lifetime maximum) and IRS Tax Topic 557: 'Not in excess of $10,000 used in a qualified first-time home purchase.' Course table states $10,000 — correct.

facts.claim: Roth IRAs have no required minimum distributions during the original owner's lifetime.
facts.source: IRS Publication 590-B: 'If you are the original owner of a Roth IRA, you don't have to take distributions regardless of your age.' IRS RMD FAQs: 'The RMD rules do not apply to Roth IRAs or Designated Roth accounts while the owner is alive.' Course claim verified.

facts.claim: A Traditional IRA forces distributions out from 'your mid-seventies' (course wording, Stage 3 Module 11 and Stage 5 Module 07).
facts.corrected_to: Age 73. IRS: 'you generally must start taking withdrawals from your traditional IRA, SEP IRA, SIMPLE IRA, and retirement plan accounts when you reach age 73.' (Rises to 75 in 2033 under SECURE 2.0.) The glossary should say 73, not 'mid-seventies'.
facts.source: IRS 'Retirement plan and IRA required minimum distributions FAQs'

facts.claim: There is no income limit on converting a Traditional IRA to a Roth IRA; the old $100,000 MAGI cap was removed in 2010 and never reinstated.
facts.source: IRS Publication 590 (2010), What's New: 'Beginning in 2010, the modified AGI and filing status requirements for converting a traditional IRA to a Roth IRA are eliminated.' Current Publication 590-A carries no MAGI limit on conversions. Course claim (Module 11) verified.

facts.claim: A Roth conversion cannot be undone — recharacterization was eliminated for conversions made in 2018 or later.
facts.source: IRS Publication 590-A: 'No recharacterizations of conversions made in 2018 or later.' Course claim verified.

facts.claim: The pro-rata rule aggregates ALL traditional, SEP and SIMPLE IRAs, valued as of 31 December of the conversion year; Roth IRAs and employer plan balances such as a 401(k) are excluded from that value.
facts.source: Instructions for Form 8606, line 6: 'Enter the total value of all your traditional IRAs as of December 31, ... plus any outstanding rollovers' — covering traditional, SEP and SIMPLE IRAs only; Roth IRAs are handled separately in Part III and employer plans are not included. Course claim (Module 11) verified.

facts.claim: Pre-tax IRA money can be rolled into a current employer's qualified plan (401(k)), which is the standard fix for the pro-rata problem before a backdoor Roth.
facts.source: IRS Rollover Chart (irs.gov/pub/irs-tege/rollover_chart.pdf) — Traditional IRA to Qualified Plan: Yes. Course action step verified.

facts.claim: Form 8606 must be filed to report nondeductible traditional IRA contributions and Roth conversions; failing to file carries a $50 penalty and overstating nondeductible contributions carries a $100 penalty.
facts.source: Instructions for Form 8606: 'you must pay a $50 penalty, unless you can show reasonable cause' for failure to file; '$100 penalty' for overstating nondeductible contributions. The course tells readers to file 8606 but does not state the penalties — worth adding.

facts.claim: Each Roth conversion carries its own 5-year clock; converted amounts withdrawn before age 59-1/2 within that period are subject to the 10% additional tax.
facts.source: IRS Publication 590-B — distribution of converted amounts within the 5-year period beginning with the conversion year is subject to the 10% additional tax on early distributions. Course claim (Stage 5, Module 07) verified.

facts.claim: Most non-spouse beneficiaries must empty an inherited Roth IRA within 10 years, by 31 December of the year containing the 10th anniversary of the owner's death; this applies to deaths after 31 December 2019.
facts.source: IRS Publication 590-B: 'The 10-year rule requires the IRA beneficiaries who are not taking life expectancy payments to withdraw the entire balance of the IRA by December 31 of the year containing the 10th anniversary of the owner's death.' IRS Notice 2024-35 confirms the SECURE Act replaced the 5-year rule with a 10-year rule for most designated beneficiaries of owners dying after 31 December 2019; eligible designated beneficiaries (surviving spouse, minor child, disabled, chronically ill, or not more than 10 years younger) are excepted. Course claim verified.

facts.claim: Course claim: 'Money you pull out of a Roth cannot be put back — you do not get that contribution room again, ever.'
facts.corrected_to: Overstated as an absolute. A distribution can be returned via a 60-day rollover: 'You have 60 days from the date you receive an IRA or retirement plan distribution to roll it over,' limited to 'only one rollover from an IRA to another (or the same) IRA in any 12-month period, regardless of the number of IRAs you own,' aggregating all traditional, SEP, SIMPLE and Roth IRAs. Beyond 60 days the course's statement is correct. The glossary should state the 60-day / one-per-12-months carve-out.
facts.source: IRS 'Rollovers of retirement plan and IRA distributions'

facts.claim: The 2026 401(k) elective deferral limit is $24,500 and the total annual additions limit (the mega-backdoor ceiling) is $72,000.
facts.source: IRS IR-2025-111 ($24,500 deferral limit) and Notice 2025-67, section 415(c)(1)(A) ($72,000). Course figures in Module 11 verified.

facts.claim: For 2026, catch-up contributions must be designated Roth if the participant's prior-year (2025) wages from the employer sponsoring the plan exceeded $150,000.
facts.source: IRS Notice 2025-67: 'The Roth catch-up wage threshold for 2025, which under section 414(v)(7)(A) is used to determine whether an individual's catch-up contributions to an applicable employer plan ... for 2026 must be designated as Roth contributions, is increased from $145,000 to $150,000.' The course's phrasing ('exceeded $150,000 in the prior year') matches the IRS construction exactly. Note the statute uses FICA wages from that employer, so a self-employed person with no such wages is not caught.

facts.claim: Unused 529 funds can be rolled into the beneficiary's Roth IRA, subject to a $35,000 lifetime limit, a 15-year account-age requirement, a 5-year contribution look-back, and the annual Roth contribution limit; effective for distributions after 31 December 2023.
facts.source: IRS Tax Topic 313 (Qualified tuition programs): 'subject to the Roth IRA annual contribution limit and a $35,000 lifetime limit'; account 'open for at least 15 years'; 'may not exceed the amount contributed to the QTP (and attributable earnings) before the 5 year period ending on the date of the distribution'; 'Effective with respect to distributions made after Dec. 31, 2023.' Must be a direct trustee-to-trustee transfer. Course (Stage 5, Module 11) says 'since 2024 ... under specific limits and conditions' — correct but vague; the glossary should state $35,000 and the 15-year rule.

facts.claim: There is no income limit on making a nondeductible Traditional IRA contribution — income only limits the deduction. (The premise of the backdoor Roth.)
facts.source: IRS IR-2025-111 frames the 2026 income ranges as 'phase-out ranges for determining deductibility'; Instructions for Form 8606 exist specifically to report 'nondeductible contributions to a traditional IRA', and Pub 590-A imposes only a compensation requirement, not an income ceiling, on the contribution itself. Course claim verified.

facts.claim: Course claim (Stage 3, Module 11): 'Congress was told about [the backdoor Roth] in plain language in the 2017 tax bill's conference report and chose to leave it alone.'
facts.source: I confirmed that H. Rept. 115-466 (TCJA conference report, govinfo.gov) contains the section 'Repeal of special rule permitting recharacterization of IRA contributions (sec. 1501 of the House bill, sec. 13611 of the Senate amendment, and sec. 408A of the Code)' at p. 288, but neither govinfo's HTML nor its PDF returned the explanatory footnote text, and congress.gov blocks automated fetching. Do NOT assert the 'Congress was told in plain language' framing on the glossary page without a human reading p. 288 of the report; state the legal position (no MAGI limit on conversions) instead, which is fully sourced.

facts.claim: Course claim (Stage 3, Module 10): a Roth 401(k) at work 'follows different, stricter withdrawal rules' than a Roth IRA.
facts.source: Directionally right — designated Roth accounts do not use the Roth IRA contributions-first ordering, and in-service access is plan-dependent — but the IRS 'Designated Roth accounts in retirement plans' page returned 404 on fetch and I did not confirm the mechanism in Publication 575. Either verify against Pub 575 before stating a mechanism, or keep the glossary wording at the level of 'different rules; check your plan.'

facts.claim: ADJACENT ERROR FOUND: FL Stage 5, Module 12 states the qualified charitable distribution cap is 'up to $108,000/year in 2026'.
facts.corrected_to: $111,000 for 2026. IRS Notice 2025-67: 'The aggregate amount of qualified charitable distributions that are not includible in gross income under section 408(d)(8)(A) is increased from $108,000 to $111,000.' $108,000 was the 2025 figure. This is a Traditional IRA fact, not a Roth one, but it is a wrong 2026 number sitting in the same course cluster and should be fixed in stage-5-wealth.html.

facts.claim: COURSE CITATION GAP (not a wrong number, but a sourcing defect the glossary must not inherit). TA Stage 1 Module 5 puts a direct quotation in quote marks — support and resistance are 'nearly but not quite synonymous with demand and supply' — and attributes it only to 'one classic technical analysis text'. The source is almost certainly Edwards & Magee, Chapter 13, but I could not confirm the exact wording against the book: archive.org full-text search, Open Library search-inside, HathiTrust full-text search and Google Books are all robots-disallowed or blocked from this environment, and the one reachable full-text scan truncates before Chapter 13. Do NOT reproduce this as a verbatim quotation on the glossary page unless someone checks a copy of the book and cites chapter and page. Either name the source properly or paraphrase without quote marks. hustlin.org's about.html publicly commits to citing source and year, so an unnamed quoted source is a live inconsistency.

facts.claim: Edwards & Magee's formal definitions, widely reproduced as: support is 'buying, either actual or potential, in sufficient volume to prevent any further downward movement in prices for an appreciable period'; resistance is 'selling, either actual or potential, in sufficient volume to satisfy all bids, thereby preventing prices from going any higher for a while.'
facts.source: Reproduced in Stuart Evens, 'Support And Resistance', Technical Analysis of Stocks & Commodities v17:1 (Jan 1999), pp. 55-58, hosted at fidelity.com — https://www.fidelity.com/bin-public/060_www_fidelity_com/documents/SupportandResistance.pdf. This is a SECONDARY source quoting the book; the book itself was not reachable. Safe to paraphrase the substance (support = demand concentration halting a decline; resistance = supply concentration halting an advance), unsafe to publish as a verbatim quote.

facts.claim: COURSE CLAIM, TA Stage 1 Module 7 and Stage 2: a breakout through support or resistance is credible when volume is 'roughly 1.5 to 2 times the average daily volume'. No standard-setting body, exchange, regulator, or original author publishes this threshold. Every source restating it is commercial or secondary. The course already hedges it ('often cited as roughly'); the glossary must keep an equivalent hedge and must never state it as a rule or a test.
facts.source: Searched for any primary/authoritative origin; only commercial trading sites returned. Course text: /mnt/user-data/uploads/Hustlin-main/TA Course/stage-1-chart-basics.html, Module 07

facts.claim: COURSE CLAIM, TA Stage 1 Module 5: support and resistance are 'usually zones a few percent wide, not exact prices'. No primary source sets a width. This is a hedged rule of thumb and is fine to repeat as such — but do NOT convert 'a few percent' into a specific number or range on the glossary page, because there is nothing to cite behind it.
facts.source: No standard-setting body publishes a zone width. Course text: TA Course/stage-1-chart-basics.html, Module 05

facts.claim: COURSE CLAIM, TA Stage 1 Module 5: a level needs at least two reversals to be drawn, and 'the more times price has respected a level, and the more volume that traded there, the more significant that level tends to be'. The two-touch minimum is definitional (a horizontal line needs two points). The 'more touches = more significant' claim is a convention with no primary authority and mixed academic support — the only reachable statement of it is secondary.
facts.source: Stuart Evens, Technical Analysis of Stocks & Commodities v17:1 (Jan 1999) — secondary. https://www.fidelity.com/bin-public/060_www_fidelity_com/documents/SupportandResistance.pdf

facts.claim: If the glossary page mentions placing a stop-loss just below support (the standard practical use of the concept), the mechanics are: a stop order becomes a MARKET order once the stop price is reached; the stop price is NOT the guaranteed execution price; the execution price can deviate significantly from the stop price in a fast-moving market; and a stop can be triggered by a short-term intraday move at a price substantially worse than the stock's closing price for the day.
facts.source: SEC Office of Investor Education and Advocacy, 'Investor Bulletin: Stop, Stop-Limit, and Trailing Stop Orders', 13 July 2017 — https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins-15

facts.claim: Support and resistance is not a regulated, standardized, or regulator-defined term. No SEC, FINRA or CFTC publication defines it or sets any threshold for it — Investor.gov's own day-trading entry does not mention technical analysis, charts, or chart levels at all, and warns only that 'Day trading is extremely risky and can result in substantial financial losses in a very short period of time.' This supports the site's standing educational-commentary disclaimer and means no claim on this page should be framed as an official or authoritative standard.
facts.source: SEC Investor.gov glossary entry, 'Day Trading' — https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/glossary/day-trading

facts.claim: Definition: a yield curve is inverted when short-term Treasury yields exceed long-term ones — equivalently, a negative term spread. Taught in EconomicsCourse/stage-3-rates-central-banks-bonds.html, Module 04 'The Yield Curve'.
facts.source: San Francisco Fed Economic Letter 2018-07 (Bauer & Mertens): 'Every U.S. recession in the past 60 years was preceded by a negative term spread, that is, an inverted yield curve.' https://www.frbsf.org/research-and-insights/publications/economic-letter/2018/03/economic-forecasts-with-yield-curve/

facts.claim: CURRENT STATE (what a 2026 reader needs): the US curve is NOT inverted. 10-year minus 2-year = +0.47 percentage points and 10-year minus 3-month = +0.83 percentage points on 10 Aug 2026. Underlying Treasury par yields that day: 1 Mo 3.79, 3 Mo 3.89, 2 Yr 4.25, 10 Yr 4.72, 30 Yr 5.25 — an upward-sloping (normal) curve at every point checked.
facts.source: FRED T10Y2Y (2026-08-10 = 0.47) and T10Y3M (2026-08-10 = 0.83); cross-checked against U.S. Treasury Daily Par Yield Curve Rates, August 2026

facts.claim: The course's 'record' framing needs a 2026 update: the 2022–2024 inversion has NOT been followed by an NBER-dated recession. NBER's most recent business-cycle turning points remain the February 2020 peak and April 2020 trough — no US recession has been dated since. The historical 6-to-24-month lead window measured from the July 2022 inversion (Jan 2023 – Jul 2024) has fully elapsed, and so has the window from the September 2024 un-inversion.
facts.corrected_to: As of 11 August 2026 the most recent inversion signal (2022–2024) has not been followed by a recession within its historical lead time. The glossary page must say the curve is currently normal and that the last inversion has so far not produced a dated recession — not repeat the course's implicit 'the record is intact' framing.
facts.source: NBER Business Cycle Dating (most recent peak Feb 2020, trough Apr 2020) https://www.nber.org/research/business-cycle-dating

facts.claim: Course claim: 'the lag is long and highly variable — historically anywhere from roughly six months to two years between inversion and recession.' Also stated as '6–24 months, highly variable' in the stage-4 leading-indicator table.
facts.source: San Francisco Fed Economic Letter 2018-07 (Bauer & Mertens): 'The delay between the term spread turning negative and the beginning of a recession has ranged between 6 and 24 months.'

facts.claim: Course claim: 'the 3-month version has the stronger academic record' (10y−3m vs 10y−2y).
facts.source: San Francisco Fed Economic Letter 2018-20, Bauer & Mertens, 27 Aug 2018: 'The traditional 10y–3m spread performs better than the other three spreads by a slight margin' — with their own caveat that 'all of these term spreads are fairly accurate predictors... the differences in forecasting accuracy are small.' https://www.frbsf.org/research-and-insights/publications/economic-letter/2018/08/information-in-yield-curve-about-future-recessions/

facts.claim: Course claim: inversion 'has produced false signals.' The primary count: one false positive, in the mid-1960s, over the 60 years to 2018. Separately, the 10y−3m spread fell to similarly low levels in 1995 and 1998 without a recession following soon after.
facts.source: SF Fed Economic Letter 2018-07: 'had only one false positive, in the mid-1960s, when an inversion was followed by an economic slowdown but not an official recession'; SF Fed Blog, Bauer & Mertens, 27 Feb 2019 (1995 and 1998 levels) https://www.frbsf.org/research-and-insights/blog/sf-fed-blog/2019/02/27/did-yield-curve-flip-will-economy-dip/

facts.claim: Course claim: 'recessions have tended to begin AFTER the curve un-inverts and returns to a normal slope, not while it is inverted.' Verified by deriving sign changes from Treasury daily par yields against NBER peak dates for the last three recessions: 10y−3m turned positive by 31 Jan 2001 (peak March 2001); both spreads were positive by 7 June 2007 (peak December 2007); 10y−3m turned positive on 11 Oct 2019 (peak February 2020).
facts.source: Derived from U.S. Treasury Daily Par Yield Curve Rates (Jan 2001, Jun 2007, Oct 2019) and NBER business-cycle peak dates. No single Fed publication stating the pattern was located; the derivation is from primary data on both sides.

facts.claim: Most recent 10y−2y inversion episode: first (one-day) inversion 1 April 2022 (2 Yr 2.44 vs 10 Yr 2.39); persistent inversion from 5–6 July 2022 (5 Jul: both 2.82; 6 Jul: 2 Yr 2.97 vs 10 Yr 2.93); ended 4 September 2024, the first day 10 Yr (3.77) exceeded 2 Yr (3.76). Day-by-day continuity across the whole span was not checked, only the endpoints.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Daily Par Yield Curve Rates, monthly tables for April 2022, July 2022 and September 2024 https://home.treasury.gov/resource-center/data-chart-center/interest-rates/TextView?type=daily_treasury_yield_curve

facts.claim: Most recent 10y−3m inversion episode: first negative day 18 Oct 2022 (10 Yr 4.01 vs 3 Mo 4.04); sustained from 25 Oct 2022 (4.10 vs 4.14); last negative day 12 Dec 2024 (4.32 vs 4.35); positive from 13 Dec 2024 (4.40 vs 4.34).
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Daily Par Yield Curve Rates, monthly tables for October 2022 and December 2024

facts.claim: IMPORTANT AND NEWER THAN THE COURSE TEXT: the 10y−3m spread went negative again at points during 2025, after un-inverting in December 2024, with no recession following. Examples from Treasury daily data: 3 Mar 2025 (10 Yr 4.16 vs 3 Mo 4.35 = −0.19), 4 Apr 2025 (4.01 vs 4.28 = −0.27), 16 Oct 2025 (3.99 vs 4.02 = −0.03). The 10y−2y spread stayed positive on every 2025 and 2026 date checked.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Daily Par Yield Curve Rates, monthly tables for Feb/Mar/Apr/Jul/Oct 2025

facts.claim: Deepest readings of the 2022–2024 episode: 10y−2y reached −1.08 percentage points on 3 July 2023 (2 Yr 4.94, 10 Yr 3.86); 10y−3m reached −1.89 percentage points on 4 May 2023 (3 Mo 5.26, 10 Yr 3.37). Troughs identified from the three candidate months sampled (March, May, July 2023).
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Daily Par Yield Curve Rates, monthly tables for March, May and July 2023

facts.claim: The New York Fed publishes a recession-probability model built on the yield curve: it uses the term spread to compute the probability of recession twelve months ahead. Latest published reading: July 2026, spread 0.7822 percentage points, probability 15.19 per cent.
facts.source: NY Fed, 'The Yield Curve as a Leading Indicator' https://www.newyorkfed.org/research/capital_markets/ycfaq and the data file 'Probability of US Recession Predicted by Treasury Spread' https://www.newyorkfed.org/medialibrary/media/research/capital_markets/prob_rec.pdf

facts.claim: Attribution of the model: Arturo Estrella and Frederic S. Mishkin, 'The Yield Curve as a Predictor of U.S. Recessions', Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Current Issues in Economics and Finance, Vol. 2 No. 7, June 1996. Uses the 10-year note minus 3-month bill spread, forecasting four quarters ahead. Their published probability table: spread +1.21 → 5%; +0.76 → 10%; +0.46 → 15%; +0.22 → 20%; +0.02 → 25%; −0.17 → 30%; −0.50 → 40%; −0.82 → 50%; −1.13 → 60%; −1.46 → 70%; −1.85 → 80%; −2.40 → 90%.
facts.source: Estrella & Mishkin (1996), NY Fed Current Issues in Economics and Finance 2(7) https://www.newyorkfed.org/medialibrary/media/research/current_issues/ci2-7.pdf

facts.claim: Caveat worth carrying: the Federal Reserve Board's own research argues the near-term forward spread (six-quarter-ahead forward rate minus the current 3-month bill) dominates the long-term spread. Once it is included, 'the estimated effect of the competing long-term spread on the probability of recession is economically small and not statistically different from zero.'
facts.source: Engstrom & Sharpe, '(Don't Fear) The Yield Curve', FEDS Notes, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, 28 June 2018 https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/notes/feds-notes/dont-fear-the-yield-curve-20180628.htm

facts.claim: The FRED series a reader should chart are T10Y2Y ('10-Year Treasury Constant Maturity Minus 2-Year Treasury Constant Maturity') and T10Y3M ('10-Year ... Minus 3-Month ...'), both daily, in percent, not seasonally adjusted — the two series the course's action steps point students to.
facts.source: FRED series pages https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/T10Y2Y and https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/T10Y3M

facts.claim: US recessions are dated by the NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee, not by the two-consecutive-quarters-of-negative-GDP rule; the committee waits for data and announces turning points well after the fact. Concrete case: the April 2020 trough was announced on 19 July 2021 — a 15-month lag. (The course's stage-1 line 'sometimes a year or more after the fact' holds.)
facts.source: NBER Business Cycle Dating https://www.nber.org/research/business-cycle-dating and NBER announcement of 19 July 2021 https://www.nber.org/news/business-cycle-dating-committee-announcement-july-19-2021
